concepts.name: General Purpose Technology (GPT)
concepts.definition: A technology characterized by three features: used as input across many downstream sectors, subject to ongoing technical improvement, and generating positive externalities to downstream innovators. The defining insight is that GPT value accrues through cascading complementary innovation downstream, not from the technology itself.
concepts.canonical_source: Bresnahan & Trajtenberg, "General Purpose Technologies 'Engines of Growth'," Journal of Econometrics (1995)
concepts.originator: Timothy Bresnahan and Manuel Trajtenberg, 1995
concepts.what_it_captures: First order (primary innovation) plus the mechanism linking it to downstream application. Explicitly models that GPT productivity depends on complementary innovation in downstream sectors.
concepts.where_it_differs: GPT theory emphasizes innovation complementarities and coordination failures as the mechanism; doesn't specifically name overcapacity or malinvestment as a distinct second-order phase.

concepts.name: Productivity Paradox / Solow Paradox
concepts.definition: The empirical puzzle that massive investment in information technology (especially computers, 1970s-1980s) failed to show corresponding productivity gains in national statistics, despite widespread deployment. Partially resolved through organizational restructuring and intangible capital accumulation.
concepts.canonical_source: Robert Solow, quip cited in Brynjolfsson; Erik Brynjolfsson, 1993 paper codifying the term
concepts.originator: Robert Solow (observation); Erik Brynjolfsson (formal analysis), circa 1990-1993
concepts.what_it_captures: The lag between 1st order (computer/IT invention) and observable 3rd order value (productivity gains). Shows the 2nd order reorganization phase where investment occurs without measured return.
concepts.where_it_differs: The Solow paradox focuses on measurement and learning lags rather than on malinvestment or overcapacity as productive. It emphasizes that the technology works, but its benefits accrue only after organizational adaptation.

concepts.name: Productivity J-Curve
concepts.discipline: Economics of intangible capital and technology adoption
concepts.definition: A model showing that adoption of a General Purpose Technology initially produces a dip or plateau in measured productivity (as firms invest in complementary intangible capital), followed by accelerating productivity gains once those complementary investments mature. The curve's shape reflects unmeasured intangible capital accumulation.
concepts.canonical_source: Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson, "The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies," NBER Working Paper (2018)
concepts.originator: Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock, Chad Syverson, 2018
concepts.what_it_captures: Exactly the lag mechanism: first 1st order innovation, then 2nd order (flat/declining measured productivity while intangible capital accumulates), then 3rd order (rapid value realization). The dip is not failure, it's reorganization cost.
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on intangible capital and measurement bias rather than speculation or overcapacity. Doesn't explain whether overlays third-order value capture to different players.

concepts.name: Complementary Organizational Capital
concepts.discipline: Economics of innovation and firm performance
concepts.definition: Intangible assets specific to a firm's operations—organizational processes, worker training, incentive systems, business model design—that must be built or restructured to unlock value from new technologies. Empirically, combination of IT capital with organizational capital shows disproportionately high productivity.
concepts.canonical_source: Brynjolfsson & Hitt, "Intangible Assets: Computers and Organizational Capital," Brookings Papers on Economic Activity (2002); earlier: "Computing Productivity: Firm-Level Evidence"
concepts.originator: Erik Brynjolfsson and Lorin M. Hitt, circa 2000-2002
concepts.what_it_captures: The mechanism of the 2nd order: reorganization isn't incidental, it's essential and measurably productive. Shows that productivity gains are impossible without it.
concepts.where_it_differs: Strictly organizational/firm-level; doesn't address economy-wide overcapacity, malinvestment, or inter-firm value transfer. Assumes reorganization succeeds; doesn't model failed experiments or bubble waste.

concepts.name: Complementary Assets / Cospecialized Assets
concepts.definition: Assets (tangible or intangible) required to make an innovation valuable in use. Cospecialized assets have mutual dependence: the asset depends on the innovation, and the innovation depends on the asset. Value capture from an innovation depends critically on who owns or controls complementary assets.
concepts.canonical_source: Teece, Pisano & Shuen, "Dynamic Capabilities and Strategic Management," Strategic Management Journal (1997); earlier Teece work on appropriability
concepts.originator: David Teece (originator of appropriability framework, 1980s); formalized with Pisano & Shuen, 1997
concepts.what_it_captures: Explains why different players capture value: those who control complementary assets, not innovators. Helps explain why 3rd order businesses (AWS) capture more value than 2nd order infrastructure builders (fiber companies).
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not directly address the 1st/2nd/3rd order distinction or the lag phenomenon. It explains value distribution within a single wave, not across waves.

concepts.name: Technology Diffusion Lag / Adoption Lag
concepts.discipline: Economics of innovation and organizational behavior
concepts.definition: The typically long period between initial availability of a technology and widespread productive adoption. Arises from organizational learning requirements, adjustment costs, complementary investment thresholds, and barriers to replicating frontier practices. Creates divergence between early adopters and laggards.
concepts.canonical_source: Paul David, "The Dynamo and the Computer: An Historical Perspective on the Modern Productivity Paradox," American Economic Review (1990); Berlingieri et al. OECD work on frontier/laggard divergence (2020s)
concepts.originator: Paul David (1990); modern documentation by Berlingieri, Bartelsman, others (2010s-2020s)
concepts.what_it_captures: Directly models the lag between 1st and 3rd order. David's electricity example: group-drive factories (1880s) → unit-drive reorganization (1920s) = 40-year lag. Shows lag is structural, not transitional.
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on organizational learning and heterogeneous adoption. Does not characterize the 2nd order specifically as bubble/malinvestment or address value-capture patterns across orders.

concepts.name: Co-invention
concepts.discipline: Economics of innovation and technology strategy
concepts.definition: The requirement that adoption of a new GPT triggers simultaneous invention and development of complementary technologies, business models, and organizational practices by downstream firms. Not a one-time adaptation but an ongoing cascade of innovations.
concepts.canonical_source: Bresnahan & Trajtenberg (1995) concept of 'innovational complementarities'; elaborated in downstream transmission studies
concepts.originator: Implicit in Bresnahan & Trajtenberg (1995); term and explicit modeling developed by subsequent scholars
concepts.what_it_captures: Captures the idea that 2nd and 3rd order are not passive exploitation of 1st order—they require active invention. The conveyor belt wasn't invented by electrification; it was invented by factory engineers once electricity enabled it.
concepts.where_it_differs: Doesn't address whether co-invention is speculative/wasteful or concentrated/productive, or whether early co-invention is malinvestment.

concepts.name: Intangible Capital Accumulation
concepts.definition: Growth in firms' stocks of non-physical, non-financial capital: organizational processes, business model design, software, worker skills, brand value, and data. Accumulation is slow, difficult to measure, and subject to spillovers. Critical to explaining productivity lags and measurement bias.
concepts.canonical_source: Corrado, Hulten & Sichel on intangible capital measurement; Brynjolfsson on J-curve; OECD Intangible Capital research
concepts.originator: Multiple scholars; Carol Corrado, Charles Hulten, Daniel Sichel formalized measurement; 2000s onward
concepts.what_it_captures: The hidden 2nd order: firms and economy are building productive capacity (intangible) that doesn't show up in official GDP, productivity, or capital stock measures. Explains why measured output appears flat while real reorganization is underway.
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on measurement/real accumulation vs. malinvestment. Doesn't distinguish productive intangibles from speculative waste.

concepts.name: Malinvestment / Productive Bubbles
concepts.discipline: Economics of bubbles and business cycles (Austrian school + modern finance)
concepts.definition: Investment in assets whose long-run productive value is far below capital deployed, often triggered by mispricing (low interest rates, speculative euphoria). Paradoxically, malinvestment can create real, durable productive capacity that later generations exploit (e.g., excess fiber optic cables become foundation for cloud computing).
concepts.canonical_source: Austrian business cycle theory tradition; modern treatment: Ravi Dharmarajah & John Authers on 'productive bubbles'; recent fiber optic case studies
concepts.originator: Austrian school (Mises, Hayek); popularized by modern finance writers; Dharmarajah/Authers formalize productive bubble concept (2020s)
concepts.what_it_captures: The 2nd order often is malinvestment: dot-com firms burned capital, telecom companies overbuild fiber (95% capacity, 35% use). But the overbuild was productive: it enabled cloud computing later. Resolves apparent paradox.
concepts.where_it_differs: Austrian school theory does NOT align well with GPT/complementary-innovation framing. It explains malinvestment as monetary/credit-cycle error, not as a necessary phase of technology adoption. Requires integration with GPT theory.

concepts.name: Creative Destruction
concepts.discipline: Economics of innovation and growth (Schumpeterian tradition)
concepts.definition: Industrial mutation wherein innovation incessantly destroys old products and firms while simultaneously creating new ones, new employment, and new value. New entrants and new technologies typically displace incumbents; each wave of destruction is a wave of creation.
concepts.canonical_source: Joseph Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942); modern: Gort & Klepper (1982), Christensen (1997) on disruptive innovation
concepts.originator: Joseph Schumpeter, 1942; reframed as 'disruptive innovation' by Clayton Christensen, 1997
concepts.what_it_captures: Explains why value accrues to different players across orders: incumbent firms (holders of 1st/2nd order assets) are often displaced by new entrants (3rd order) with fresh organizational models and asset bundles. Destruction of old is creation of new.
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not specifically model the lag structure (1st → 2nd → 3rd) or the role of complementary innovation and reorganization. It's a value-displacement mechanism, not a technology-adoption-lag mechanism.

concepts.name: Techno-economic paradigm (TEP)
concepts.definition: A complex collective model of best economic, technological and organizational practice that emerges during a technological revolution—comprising shared beliefs about cost structures, opportunity spaces, and organizational forms suited to the new technology cluster.
concepts.originator: Christopher Freeman and Carlota Perez, 1980s–2000s
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002)
concepts.what_it_captures: The 1st order (primary innovation) AND the institutional/organizational conditions that enable its deployment. Each paradigm shift requires learning not just new machines but new ways to organize production, consumption, and finance.
concepts.where_it_differs: Perez emphasizes that the paradigm is not just the technology itself but the entire ecosystem of cost-structure changes, business organization, and institutional arrangements that make the technology productive. The operator's framing separates 'primary innovation' from 'reorganisation,' but Perez treats reorganisation as intrinsic to each paradigm shift.

concepts.name: Great surges of development
concepts.definition: 50–60 year cycles in which a technological revolution and its paradigm propagate across the economy, causing structural shifts in production, distribution, communication, consumption, and society. Perez identifies five: Industrial Revolution (1771–1829), Steam & Railways (1829–1873), Steel-Electricity-Engineering (1875–1918), Oil-Auto-Mass Production (1908–1974), Information & Telecommunications (1971–present).
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez, formally codified in 2002; builds on Kondratiev (1925) and Schumpeter
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002)
concepts.what_it_captures: The full trajectory from primary invention through diffusion, including the lag and the different winners/captors at each stage. Captures the multi-decadal time horizon and the structural economy-wide reorganization.
concepts.where_it_differs: Perez structures this in two main phases (installation + deployment) with sub-phases, rather than the operator's three-stage ('primary', 'reorganisation', 'value capture') model. Perez's framework is cyclical and recurring; the operator's framing is more causal/sequential.

concepts.name: Installation phase / Deployment phase (turning-point model)
concepts.definition: Installation (irruption + frenzy, ~25–30 years): a new technology enters, financial capital funds rapid exploration and infrastructure build, speculation drives overinvestment, asset valuations detach from productive use. Deployment (synergy + maturity, ~25–30 years): after a turning-point crash, production capital dominates, infrastructure is used productively, technology diffuses broadly, prosperity spreads. The turning-point crisis forces recoupling of finance and production.
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez (2002)
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002); Fred Wilson's 2015 synthesis on AVC
concepts.what_it_captures: The operator's '1st and 2nd order' map roughly to installation (new tech + forced reorganisation/overcapacity). The operator's '3rd order' maps to deployment (where the overcapacity enables new businesses). The turning-point crash (the operator's 'lag') is the critical transition mechanism.
concepts.where_it_differs: Perez's model includes explicit sub-phases (irruption, frenzy, synergy, maturity) and treats the crash as functionally necessary, not accidental. The operator treats the '2nd order' as waste/malinvestment in isolation; Perez treats it as structurally enabling. The operator emphasizes unpredictability; Perez emphasizes pattern recurrence (50–60 year cycles).

concepts.name: Financial capital vs. Production capital
concepts.definition: Financial capital: footloose money seeking speculative returns, short time horizon, driven by novelty and hype, abundant in installation when uncertainty is high. Production capital: rooted in competence and geography, seeks productive returns through goods/services, longer time horizon, cautious, abundant only after infrastructure viability is proven.
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez (2002)
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002)
concepts.what_it_captures: Why bubbles form (financial capital overestimates returns), why crashes occur (financial capital withdraws), and why deployment succeeds (production capital is more stable and aligned with actual demand). Explains the lag between 1st and 3rd order: financial capital rushes in immediately after invention; production capital waits for clarity on ROI, which only emerges after the crash resets expectations.
concepts.where_it_differs: This distinction is unique to Perez and is not a named concept elsewhere in the literature. It explains mechanism; most cycle theories do not.

concepts.name: Kondratiev wave / Long wave
concepts.definition: A recurring economic cycle of approximately 50–60 years, driven by waves of technological innovation and capital investment. Each wave comprises growth, stagnation, depression, and recovery phases, with radical clusters of innovations (general-purpose technologies) as the driving force.
concepts.originator: Nikolay Kondratiev (1925, 'The Major Economic Cycles')
concepts.canonical_source: Kondratiev (1925); Schumpeter (1939) popularized and renamed them 'Kondratieff Waves'
concepts.what_it_captures: The 50–60 year structural cycle that encompasses the operator's entire 1st + 2nd + 3rd order cascade. Kondratiev attributed cycles to technology; later scholars (Freeman, Perez) added institutional change as a co-driver. Captures the macro pattern but not the financial/institutional mechanism.
concepts.where_it_differs: Kondratiev waves are macro-level observations of boom/bust cycles; Perez's framework explains the micro-mechanism (financial vs production capital, paradigm shifts). Kondratiev did not distinguish between types of capital or explain why crashes enable subsequent deployment. Kondratiev waves are debated among mainstream economists; Perez's framework is more accepted in heterodox and innovation-studies circles.

concepts.name: Creative destruction vs. Creative construction (synergy phase)
concepts.definition: Creative destruction (installation phase): old industries and incumbent firms are displaced by radical innovations; competitive pressure is intense; many experiments fail. Creative construction (deployment phase): the paradigm spreads predictably; focus shifts from invention to optimization; incumbent firms adapt or new firms capture application layers; cooperation and standardization dominate.
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez (2002); terminology influenced by Schumpeter's 'creative destruction' (1942)
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002)
concepts.what_it_captures: Explains why the operator calls the 2nd order 'disruption' and the 3rd order 'value creation'—they are two fundamentally different economic logics. Installation is chaotic; deployment is synergistic.
concepts.where_it_differs: Perez treats these as sequential phases within a single surge, not separate phenomena. The operator treats them as outcomes of a single primary shock; Perez treats them as mutually constitutive—the destruction in phase 1 enables the construction in phase 2.

concepts.name: Infrastructure overbuilding / Stranded assets as scaffolding
concepts.definition: During the frenzy phase, financial capital overestimates long-term demand and overbuilds infrastructure (fiber, railways, data centers, etc.). Most investments fail; assets become 'stranded.' After the crash, production capital recognizes that this overbuilt infrastructure—though wasteful in its specific form—provides the dense backbone that enabling the next wave of application-layer innovation.
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez (2002); formalized by analysts of the dot-com boom and AI capex booms (2010s–2020s)
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002); Kedrovsky (2024 analysis on AI capex)
concepts.what_it_captures: The operator's claim that the 2nd order 'looks like waste or disruption at the time' but enables the 3rd order. Perez shows this is not accidental—bubbles serve a function. Unlit fiber from dot-com boom = infrastructure for 2000s internet boom; data centers built for speculative AI = substrate for enterprise AI deployment.
concepts.where_it_differs: Most economic theory treats bubbles as failures; Perez treats them as features. The operator treats them as contingent and wasteful; Perez treats them as structurally necessary (though painful). This is a fundamental reframing.

concepts.name: Turning-point crisis / Synergy phase transition
concepts.definition: A sharp rupture (typically a financial crash, recession, or geopolitical shock) that ends the frenzy phase and forces a recoupling between financial and production capital. Asset valuations correct; speculative firms fail; survivors are production-oriented; institutional structures adapt (regulation, corporate forms, labor markets). This crisis is not incidental but functionally necessary to shift investment from speculative to productive channels.
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez (2002)
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002)
concepts.what_it_captures: The operator's '20–50 year lag' between primary and tertiary waves. The crash is the hinge pin. Without it, financial capital would continue chasing novelty without generating productive deployment; the crash resets behavior and clears away unprofitable incumbent structures.
concepts.where_it_differs: Most business-cycle theory treats crashes as harmful shocks; Perez treats them as corrections that enable sustained growth. The operator treats the lag as mysterious; Perez explains it mechanistically through capital type transitions and institutional adaptation.

concepts.name: Golden age (prosperity diffusion phase)
concepts.definition: The middle-to-late deployment phase (synergy + early maturity) in which new technology infrastructure is fully productive, returns are stable and widely distributed, employment is high, real wages rise, and inequality often declines. The post-WWII manufacturing expansion (1945–1973) is Perez's canonical example.
concepts.originator: Carlota Perez (2002); term 'golden age' is older (economic historians); Perez applies it specifically to tech-deployment phases
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002)
concepts.what_it_captures: The operator's '3rd order' is precisely what Perez means by golden ages: 'an entirely new generation of business...that exploited that stranded infrastructure.' AWS/Azure are 3rd-order entities capturing value from 1st+2nd-order fiber and data-center infrastructure. Perez shows this pattern recurs.
concepts.where_it_differs: Perez emphasizes that the golden age is not automatic—it requires deliberate institutional adaptation (policy, regulation, labor arrangements). The operator treats it as an inevitable outcome; Perez treats it as an achievable but contingent scenario requiring active shaping by government and civil society.

concepts.name: Combinatorial (Recombinant) Innovation
concepts.definition: The process by which new technologies are constructed by recombining existing technological components, ideas, and knowledge. Innovation does not emerge from scratch but through progressive linking of pre-existing elements in novel arrangements.
concepts.originator: W. Brian Arthur (2009), Martin Weitzman (1998)
concepts.canonical_source: The Nature of Technology (Arthur, 2009); Recombinant Growth (Weitzman, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 1998)
concepts.what_it_captures: The fundamental mechanism that creates third-order innovations. Once the second-order infrastructure exists, third-order businesses recombine available technologies (fiber optics, server hardware, human knowledge) to create new services (AWS, Netflix, Cloudflare).
concepts.where_it_differs: Explains WHY third-order innovations become possible, but does not address the timing lag, the role of the second-order bubble as prerequisite, or the value-capture transfer to new actors.

concepts.name: Adjacent Possible
concepts.definition: The set of possible next states or innovations that are reachable given the current state of a system. Each actualization of a state adjacent to the current one expands the adjacent possible itself, creating new possibilities that were previously unreachable.
concepts.originator: Stuart Kauffman (complexity theory); popularized in economics by Steven Johnson
concepts.canonical_source: Stuart Kauffman's work on complex adaptive systems; Steven Johnson's Emergence and Where Good Ideas Come From
concepts.what_it_captures: Why third-order innovations appear feasible once the second-order infrastructure is in place. The infrastructure-building (overcapacity of fiber, data center expertise, cloud operating models) literally expands what is adjacent/feasible to accomplish.
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes the logical availability of innovations but does not explain the economic inefficiency of the second-order phase, the bubble dynamics, or why this adjacency is realized by new actors rather than incumbents.

concepts.name: Innovation Cascades
concepts.definition: A long series of interlinked radical innovations that emerge across institutions and countries, where each breakthrough enables or constrains the next, creating technological momentum that makes the future less predictable but enables experimentation with multiple value-creation strategies.
concepts.originator: Innovation studies literature, empirically demonstrated in biotechnology (DNA structure → genomics → proteomics → therapeutic applications)
concepts.canonical_source: Relating Business Model Innovations and Innovation Cascades: The Case of Biotechnology (2019 research in innovation journals)
concepts.what_it_captures: The exact sequence the operator describes: radical innovations radiate outward, force reorganizations, and spawn multiple successive business models each targeting different aspects of the expanded technological space.
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes the sequencing but not specifically the lag timing, the role of bubbles as cascade-drivers, or the concentration of value capture in later stages.

concepts.name: General Purpose Technologies (GPT) and the Productivity Paradox
concepts.definition: General purpose technologies (electricity, computing, internet) are broad-based innovations applicable to many sectors. The Productivity Paradox is the observation that their deployment initially causes productivity decline due to learning costs, organizational restructuring, and infrastructure adaptation, with gains only appearing after 20-40 years.
concepts.originator: Paul David (on electricity paradox); Erik Brynjolfsson (on information technology productivity paradox)
concepts.canonical_source: Paul A. David's work on the Second Industrial Revolution; 'The Productivity Paradox' (MIT Technology Review); studies on electricity/factory reorganization timing
concepts.what_it_captures: Explains the lag between first-order innovation and third-order value realization. Electric motors replaced steam engines in 1880s but factory productivity gains didn't emerge until ~1920 because reorganization around distributed power took decades.
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on organizational learning and infrastructure adaptation costs, not on the bubble/malinvestment aspects of the second order or the disruption of incumbent value capture.

concepts.name: Amara's Law
concepts.definition: An observation that societies systematically overestimate technology's short-term transformative impact while underestimating long-term effects. Technologies follow an S-curve trajectory from hype through disillusionment to eventual widespread adoption and value realization.
concepts.originator: Roy Amara (Institute for the Future), 1981
concepts.canonical_source: Roy Amara's forecasting observations (1981 onwards)
concepts.what_it_captures: The predictable underestimation of how long the second-to-third-order transition takes, and why third-order value appears to arrive unexpectedly after apparent failure of the technology.
concepts.where_it_differs: Addresses cognitive bias in prediction and adoption timing, not the economic mechanisms (overcapacity, disruption, recombination) that actually drive third-order value creation.

concepts.name: Path Dependence and Technological Lock-in
concepts.definition: Once infrastructure and institutions are built around a technology (even if sub-optimal), switching costs and network effects create self-reinforcing cycles that lock society into that technological path. Early contingent choices become determinative of long-term trajectories.
concepts.originator: W. Brian Arthur, Paul David; broader concept in institutional economics
concepts.canonical_source: Arthur's work on increasing returns; David on QWERTY and technology lock-in
concepts.what_it_captures: Explains why the second-order infrastructure (fiber networks, factory layouts, digital infrastructure) becomes determinative for what third-order innovations become possible. The locked-in infrastructure constrains the adjacent possible.
concepts.where_it_differs: Explains why old paths persist, not why new paths create concentrated value capture in the third order for new actors specifically.

concepts.name: Three Faces of Technology (Emerging, Enabling, Embedding)
concepts.definition: A framework identifying three distinct value-creation sources: Emerging (novelty and breakthrough under uncertainty), Enabling (cross-domain applications and spillovers), and Embedding (business model design and ecosystem alignment). Different actors profit from different faces.
concepts.originator: Rahul Kapoor and David J. Teece, 2021
concepts.canonical_source: Kapoor & Teece, 'Three Faces of Technology's Value Creation: Emerging, Enabling, Embedding', Strategy Science 2021
concepts.what_it_captures: Maps almost directly to the operator's three orders: Emerging = first order (invention), Enabling = second order (infrastructure that spills over to new applications), Embedding = third order (business models that capture the enabling value). Crucially, notes that value captures go to different players.
concepts.where_it_differs: Treats these as distinct value sources but less emphasis on why second-order appears wasteful/bubble-like, or on the lag/timing mechanics.

concepts.name: Technology Spillovers and Externalities
concepts.definition: The unpriced benefits that flow from innovation to actors beyond the initial innovator. Infrastructure investments (fiber, electricity grids, cloud APIs) create spillovers when later innovators leverage the same infrastructure at lower cost to create new value.
concepts.originator: Traditional concept in innovation economics; formalized in endogenous growth theory
concepts.canonical_source: NBER research on IT spillovers; knowledge spillovers literature
concepts.what_it_captures: Why third-order actors profit disproportionately: they inherit the second-order infrastructure built at sunk cost, and extract value from spillovers (free or cheap access to fiber networks, protocols, expertise, installed base).
concepts.where_it_differs: Explains efficiency gains from spillovers, but does not address the disruption aspect—why incumbents from earlier orders lose value, or the mechanisms of how bubbles create future spillovers.

concepts.name: Technological Paradigms and Trajectories
concepts.definition: A technological paradigm is an outlook and set of procedures defining relevant problems and solutions in a technology domain. Within each paradigm, technological trajectories describe the cumulative, directed path of improvement. Paradigm shifts involve discontinuities.
concepts.originator: Giovanni Dosi, building on Thomas Kuhn's scientific paradigm concept
concepts.canonical_source: Dosi, G. 'Technological Paradigms and Technological Trajectories' in Handbook of the Economics of Innovation
concepts.what_it_captures: Explains why third-order innovations are not predictable from first-order paradigm: the second-order reorganization shifts the paradigm itself, expanding what problems are addressable and what solutions are tractable.
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes paradigm continuity and discontinuity, but not specifically the bubble dynamics or value concentration in later stages.

concepts.name: Stranded/Dark Fiber and Infrastructure Overcapacity
concepts.discipline: Technology Economics, Network Economics, Industry History
concepts.definition: Unused or underutilized infrastructure built during investment booms (fiber optic cable laid but unlit; data centers built for peak demand; chip fabrication capacity). This overcapacity, initially seen as malinvestment, becomes enabling infrastructure when new applications or demand patterns emerge.
concepts.originator: Observed empirically in telecom bubble (1990s) and AI infrastructure boom (2024-2026)
concepts.canonical_source: Marketplace 'Infrastructure Lessons from the Dot-Com Bubble' (2026); historical analyses of 85-95% of laid fiber remaining dark post-2001
concepts.what_it_captures: The literal, tangible manifestation of the second-order 'overcapacity' the operator describes. Netflix/YouTube could not exist without the dark fiber that had been written off as waste. Cloud services exploit overcapacity built during prior bubbles.
concepts.where_it_differs: A specific empirical pattern rather than a theoretical framework, but shows HOW overcapacity becomes enabling: it reduces marginal cost for third-order applications to near zero.

concepts.name: Futures Wheel (also: Implications Wheel)
concepts.originator: Jerome C. Glenn, 1971 (Antioch Graduate School of Education)
concepts.definition: A visual brainstorming and mapping tool that systematically captures primary (direct), secondary (first-order indirect), and tertiary (second-order indirect) consequences of a specific change, trend, or event, arranged as concentric circles radiating from a central node. Used to reveal 'if-then' causal chains and interdependencies across multiple impact levels.
concepts.canonical_source: Jerome C. Glenn's 1971 invention, formalized in 'The Futures Wheel' methodology; spread through University of Massachusetts futures curriculum workshops in early 1970s
concepts.what_it_captures: This tool directly names and visualizes what the operator means. It explicitly organizes primary shocks (center) → secondary consequences (first ring) → tertiary consequences (second ring), with connecting lines showing how the second order enables or constrains the third order.
concepts.where_it_differs: It makes no distinction between intended/unintended, desirable/undesirable, or who captures value—it is purely structural mapping of causal consequence chains.

concepts.name: Second-Order Effects / Third-Order Effects
concepts.discipline: Systems thinking, military strategy, decision science
concepts.originator: Common usage across multiple fields; formalized as analytical terminology in military doctrine (1990s–2000s effects-based operations literature) and decision science
concepts.definition: First-order effects are direct, immediate consequences of an action. Second-order effects are consequences of first-order consequences (indirect, often delayed, harder to predict). Third-order effects are consequences of second-order effects. The higher the order, the more diffuse and difficult to attribute causally.
concepts.canonical_source: Military doctrine formalization in U.S. Air Force doctrine (AFDP 3-60) and Army effects-based operations manuals; popularized in decision-making by Ray Dalio and Wes Kao (2010s–2020s)
concepts.what_it_captures: Formally captures the layered cascade. The operator's 'primary innovation' maps to first-order effects; 'secondary reorganization/overcapacity' to second-order effects; 'tertiary businesses exploiting that infrastructure' to third-order effects.
concepts.where_it_differs: This terminology is neutral on timing and value accrual—it doesn't inherently encode that second-order is often wasteful/disruptive or that third-order captures most value. It also doesn't address the lag or the distribution of who bears vs. captures value.

concepts.name: Cascading Effects
concepts.discipline: Systems theory, ecology, infrastructure systems, military strategy
concepts.originator: Widespread across complex-systems literature; not traceable to single originator but foundational in systems dynamics (Jay Forrester) and complexity science
concepts.definition: Chain-reaction phenomenon where a change in one component triggers sequential effects through connected components. Effects spread over time, across domains/levels/generations, via directional information or material flows. Can be unidirectional or bidirectional.
concepts.canonical_source: SESYNC (Socio-Environmental Synthesis Center); military analysis of systemic impacts in protracted conflict; ecological cascade modeling
concepts.what_it_captures: Captures the mechanical notion that each order of consequence flows from the prior, and that they propagate through interconnected systems. The electricity factory-reorganization-assembly-line chain is a textbook example of cascading effects.
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not address predictability or timing. Does not explicitly separate the concept that second-order cascades are often involuntary disruptions/reallocations versus third-order being the deliberate exploitation of new capability. Uses different language ('cascade') than the operator's 'order.'

concepts.name: Unintended (Unanticipated) Consequences
concepts.originator: Robert K. Merton, 1936 ('The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action,' American Sociological Review)
concepts.definition: Outcomes of organized action that diverge from the actor's intention. Merton identified five sources: ignorance, error, immediacy of interest, basic values/worldview, and self-defeating prophecy. Core insight: purposive social action generates results outside the actor's model because social systems exceed the planner's comprehension.
concepts.canonical_source: Merton, R. K. (1936). The unanticipated consequences of purposive social action. American Sociological Review, 1, 894-904.
concepts.what_it_captures: Directly names a key feature the operator emphasizes: that second-order effects (reorganization, overcapacity, malinvestment) are often *not intended* by the first-order actors. Merton's framework explains why bubble-building actors don't plan for third-order value capture.
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on divergence between intention and outcome, not on the specific cascade of orders or on the temporal lag. Also doesn't address which order captures value—it's primarily about surprise.

concepts.name: Effects-Based Operations (EBO) / Effects Classification
concepts.originator: U.S. military doctrine development (1990s Gulf War era); formalized in Defense Department planning frameworks and joint publications
concepts.definition: Military planning methodology that works backward from desired strategic effects to tactical actions. Explicitly classifies effects as: direct/indirect, intended/unintended, first/second/third/nth-order. Indirect effects include 'cascading' (chain-reaction), 'systemic' (affecting critical interdependencies), and 'cumulative' (aggregate of many small actions).
concepts.canonical_source: U.S. Air Force Doctrine Publication 3-60 (Targeting), 2026; DTIC research papers on effects-based operations; Army effects doctrine
concepts.what_it_captures: Provides a formal military vocabulary for thinking through consequence orders and explicitly names 'cascading' and 'systemic' effects. The doctrine acknowledges that second and third-order effects are difficult/impossible to predict and that indirect effects often create unintended harm.
concepts.where_it_differs: Designed for tactical/strategic military outcomes, not economic value capture. The language of 'cascading' and 'systemic' is used interchangeably, whereas the operator distinguishes second-order (the reorganization itself) from third-order (what becomes possible after it). Does not encode 'bubble/malinvestment' as a category.

concepts.name: Leverage Points in Systems
concepts.originator: Donella H. Meadows (1997, formalized in 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System')
concepts.definition: Ranked hierarchy of 12 places where small changes can produce large system behavior shifts. Ranked from low (parameters/constants) to high (paradigm/mindset). High-leverage interventions trigger unpredictable cascading effects across the entire system because they alter the rules and goals from which all lower-order structures derive.
concepts.canonical_source: Meadows, D. H. (1997). Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System. The Donella Meadows Institute.
concepts.what_it_captures: Captures the insight that a single intervention (primary innovation) can force system reorganization (second-order) because it is a high-leverage point. Paradigm shifts particularly create cascading effects 'out of which the system arises.' Meadows notes that higher leverage points produce larger but less predictable cascades.
concepts.where_it_differs: Framework is about *where to intervene*, not about the sequence of value capture. Does not distinguish that third-order captures most value or that lag times are long. Also does not address the bubble/malinvestment character of many second-order effects.

concepts.name: Possible / Probable / Preferable Futures (with Consequence Tracing)
concepts.originator: Wendell Bell (founding theorist of futures studies field; formalized in two-volume 'Foundations of Futures Studies,' 1997–2002)
concepts.definition: Futures studies framework that distinguishes possible futures (what could happen across many scenarios), probable futures (weighted by trends/patterns), and preferable futures (valued by stakeholders). Scenario planning then traces consequences within each branch to evaluate second and third-order implications of different pathways.
concepts.canonical_source: Bell, Wendell. Foundations of Futures Studies (Volumes 1–2). Routledge, 1997–2002.
concepts.what_it_captures: The methodology of scenario planning as used in futures studies explicitly requires mapping consequences at multiple orders (first/second/third) to evaluate which futures remain robust and which collapse or pivot unexpectedly. This is how futurists formalize the operator's insight that third-order consequences often differ sharply from first-order intentions.
concepts.where_it_differs: Bell's framework focuses on *which futures are desirable*, not on the mechanics of why second-order is often a bubble or malinvestment. It is prescriptive (choosing preferable futures) rather than descriptive (mapping what actually cascades).

concepts.name: Ripple Effects Mapping (REM)
concepts.discipline: Evaluation science, public health systems, organizational change
concepts.originator: Developed as a participatory evaluation methodology in 2010s–2020s public health and systems change literature; formalized by researchers in complex systems evaluation
concepts.definition: Qualitative participatory method for capturing the wider impacts of program/system interventions. Creates visual maps of activities → intended outcomes → unintended consequences, arranged along a timeline. Deliberately captures 'downstream' and 'ripple' effects that are indirect, delayed, and unanticipated.
concepts.canonical_source: Published in BMC Medical Research Methodology, 2022; University of Bristol and University of Florida Extension programs; used in complex systems evaluation frameworks
concepts.what_it_captures: Operationalizes the insight that interventions generate unintended ripples. REM explicitly maps the difference between designed/intended effects and emergent/unanticipated consequences, which aligns with how second-order effects often surprise planners.
concepts.where_it_differs: Focused on program evaluation and capturing *all* unintended consequences (positive and negative), not on the economic value accrual pattern or the distinction that third-order is often captured by different actors.

concepts.name: The Capital Cycle
concepts.definition: A recurring four-phase pattern in capital allocation: high returns attract investment capital into an industry; abundant capital spurs competitive entry and capacity expansion; overcapacity erodes margins and reduces returns on invested capital; when returns fall below cost of capital, investors withdraw, capacity shrinks, and survivors' fortunes eventually improve. The cycle then repeats.
concepts.originator: Edward Chancellor and Marathon Asset Management portfolio managers, systematized 2002-2015; roots in earlier supply-side analysis of competitive dynamics
concepts.canonical_source: Capital Returns: Investing Through the Capital Cycle, Edward Chancellor (2015); Marathon Asset Management's Global Investment Reviews
concepts.what_it_captures: The entire 1st→2nd→3rd order sequence. Primary innovation attracts capital (1st); overinvestment and overcapacity destroy incumbent returns (2nd); but the physical infrastructure persists, later users exploit it at marginal cost (3rd). The cycle mechanically transfers wealth from Phase 2 overbuilders to Phase 3 users.
concepts.where_it_differs: The capital cycle is specifically about capital allocation behavior and competitive dynamics, not about reorganization of labor or production techniques per se. It explains *who profits when*, not *how society reorganizes*. The cycle also emphasizes that survival depends on when you enter: early investors in high-return phases lose money as competition floods in; those who stay through retrenchment and recovery capture the best returns.

concepts.name: Malinvestment (vs. Overinvestment)
concepts.definition: Capital directed into unsustainable lines of production due to artificial distortion of interest rates from credit expansion, causing entrepreneurs to misread price signals about real consumer preferences and available savings. Distinct from 'overinvestment' (too much investment in aggregate). The problem is *direction* of capital, not *volume*. When credit expansion ends, these misdirected investments are revealed as unviable.
concepts.originator: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek; Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT)
concepts.canonical_source: Human Action, L. von Mises (1949); Austrian School literature on credit expansion and boom-bust
concepts.what_it_captures: The mechanism causing the second-order 'overcapacity' phase. Credit expansion fools investors into deploying capital into ventures that wouldn't survive if interest rates reflected true time preference and savings. This explains why Phase 2 is not just 'competition' but *systematic misallocation*.
concepts.where_it_differs: Malinvestment theory emphasizes monetary policy and credit as the driver; the operator's framing is agnostic about whether the expansion is credit-driven or genuine technological optimism. Also, ABCT focuses on *liquidation* of misallocated capital during the bust, whereas the operator's examples show the capital goods themselves persist (railways, fiber) even if returns on invested capital are destroyed.

concepts.name: Financial Instability Hypothesis
concepts.definition: Prolonged financial stability and profitable operations encourage risk-taking and leverage by financial institutions and speculators. As returns increase and risk perception falls, borrowing terms ease, leverage amplifies, and the system accumulates hidden fragility. Minsky moment: a small shock triggers asset price collapse, forced deleveraging, fire sales, and systemic instability. Stability creates the seeds of instability.
concepts.originator: Hyman Minsky (1970s-1980s); revived prominently after 2008 financial crisis
concepts.canonical_source: The Financial-Instability Hypothesis, Hyman P. Minsky; Stabilizing an Unstable Economy
concepts.what_it_captures: Why the boom inevitably becomes a bust. During Phase 1 and early Phase 2, success drives leverage and risk-taking (including speculative positioning by speculators and debt-financed overbuilding). This leverage amplifies Phase 2's overcapacity crisis into a Phase 3 financial collapse. The 'bust' is not just overcapacity but a deleveraging cascade.
concepts.where_it_differs: Minsky emphasizes *financial fragility and leverage* as the transmission mechanism, whereas the operator's framing emphasizes *capital goods accumulation and productivity reorganization*. Minsky focuses on why the bust happens fast; the operator focuses on what survives the bust and who benefits. The concepts complement but address different aspects.

concepts.name: Infrastructure vs. Credit Bubbles (Asset Legacy Distinction)
concepts.definition: Infrastructure bubbles (railways, fiber optics, data centers) create large sunk capital in physical assets that cannot be easily liquidated. After the crash, the physical infrastructure remains, capacity is idle but eventually valuable as demand grows and the infrastructure operator (not the original builder) exploits it. Credit bubbles (speculative equity, CDO pyramids) destroy collateral value and leave only leverage and losses; no usable productive capacity remains.
concepts.originator: Jorda, Schularick, and Taylor (comparative bubble analysis); implicit in infrastructure cycle literature; Chancellor on capital allocation
concepts.canonical_source: Equity and Housing Bubbles and Consequences, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco; Capital Returns and historical infrastructure case studies
concepts.what_it_captures: Why the operator's examples (electricity, internet) work: they are infrastructure bubbles that left behind durable, redeployable capital. The distinction explains why Phase 3 can be so valuable—the second-order overcapacity is *physical infrastructure*, not just financial leverage or speculative positioning.
concepts.where_it_differs: This concept does not exist as a named theorem in most economic textbooks but is an observation arising from comparative bubble analysis. It directly negates the assumption that all bubbles create equally destructive aftermath; the *type* of overinvestment matters enormously for what gets left behind.

concepts.name: Overbuild-Bust-Harvest Cycle
concepts.definition: A three-phase pattern in infrastructure industries: (1) Overbuild phase—firms aggressively deploy capital in greenfield projects (railways, fiber, data centers) ahead of actual demand, often with overlapping/redundant routes or capacity, driven by first-mover advantage logic and credit availability; (2) Bust phase—utilization falls below projections, balance sheets stretch, equities collapse, many builders fail; (3) Harvest phase—idle infrastructure becomes stranded capacity; demand eventually catches up; operators or new entrants exploit cheap, abundant capacity to build new services at marginal cost.
concepts.originator: Implicit in railway history (19th c.); explicitly documented in telecom fiber boom (1990s); applied to current AI data center buildout
concepts.canonical_source: Railway and telecom infrastructure case studies; Lime (Limelights Networks) historical analysis; contemporary AI infrastructure commentary
concepts.what_it_captures: The full 1st→2nd→3rd sequence in infrastructure contexts. The 'overbuild' phase is rational given first-mover advantages and uncertainty, not irrational exuberance alone. The lag between bust and harvest is 20-50+ years. The physical residue of the overbuild is what enables phase 3 value capture.
concepts.where_it_differs: This is largely a descriptive historical pattern rather than a formal economic theory. It emphasizes *timing and sequencing* of who deploys capital versus who benefits, but does not explain the *mechanism* (capital cycle, credit distortion, Minsky dynamics, or structural capital constraints).

concepts.name: Picks and Shovels Investing
concepts.definition: Strategy of investing in suppliers of essential infrastructure and enabling tools to an emerging industry rather than betting on the industry's end-product winners. Name derives from California Gold Rush: merchants selling picks and shovels often profited more than individual miners. In modern context: during an AI boom, invest in semiconductor makers, power suppliers, cooling systems, networking equipment rather than AI software companies. Suppliers contract to multiple customers, sign long-term deals, reduce end-product concentration risk.
concepts.originator: Common Wall Street aphorism; formalized in modern investment literature by various strategists and fund managers
concepts.canonical_source: Blackstone, Needham Funds, and other infrastructure/technology investors' communications; historical references in investment community
concepts.what_it_captures: This is the *Phase 2 investment strategy*—during overcapacity buildup, picks-and-shovels suppliers (chip makers, cable manufacturers, power firms) capture better returns than either the end-product companies or the speculators. It recognizes that during boom phases, suppliers and infrastructure vendors profit more durably than final customers.
concepts.where_it_differs: Picks and shovels captures Phase 1→Phase 2 profit transfer (from end-product dreamers to hard-goods suppliers), but misses the operator's central insight: that Phase 3—once the infrastructure is mature and deployed—creates the *largest* value for completely different players (AWS, Netflix, cloud operators) who exploit stranded capacity. Picks-and-shovels investors often exit before Phase 3 crystallizes, missing the biggest gains.

concepts.name: Second-Level Thinking
concepts.definition: The practice of thinking beyond surface-level obvious conclusions to anticipate second and third-order effects of market developments. First-level thinkers see obvious trends (e.g., 'AI is growing, buy AI stocks'); second-level thinkers ask 'If that's obvious, who is already positioned? What does the market already price in? What structural shifts in capital allocation will result?'. Second-level thinking requires intellectual rigor and contrarian positioning to outperform.
concepts.originator: Howard Marks, Oaktree Capital Management, articulated in The Most Important Thing (2011)
concepts.canonical_source: The Most Important Thing: Uncommon Sense for the Thoughtful Investor, Howard Marks (2011)
concepts.what_it_captures: The *investment skill* required to profit from capital cycles. Recognizing that the phase of maximum visible returns (Phase 1-2, the boom) is precisely when you should be exiting, and that Phase 3 opportunities appear unprofitable or invisible to first-level thinkers. Second-level thinking would identify when an industry shifts from capital-attraction phase to capital-destruction phase, and rotate accordingly.
concepts.where_it_differs: This is about investor *cognition and contrarianism*, not economic mechanism. It describes the intellectual skill that allows investors to navigate the capital cycle; it does not explain *why* the cycle exists or what creates overcapacity.

concepts.name: The Three Derivatives of Innovation (Value Creation vs. Capture)
concepts.definition: Applying calculus to innovation phases: (1st derivative) velocity of experimentation (how fast are new architectures tested); (2nd derivative) acceleration toward dominant design (are competing designs converging); (3rd derivative) inflection/jerk—the inversion point where dominant design locks, transition becomes irreversible, and process innovation takes over cost curves collapse. Value *creation* is distributed across all phases via experimental startups; value *capture* concentrates at the third derivative inflection where asymmetric returns concentrate.
concepts.originator: Carter Williams, referenced in creative destruction literature; implicit in Schumpeter's work
concepts.canonical_source: The Three Derivatives of Innovation, Carter Williams (Substack, Creative Destruction newsletter)
concepts.what_it_captures: An alternative framing of the 1st→2nd→3rd order distinction using calculus language. Phase 1 (invention of electricity) is high velocity (1st derivative); Phase 2 (reorganization, overbuilding of factories and infrastructure) is high acceleration toward dominant designs (2nd derivative); Phase 3 (assembly line, WWII production capacity, cheap cars) is the inflection point (3rd derivative) where returns concentrate. Early-phase investors fund creation; later-phase operators capture concentrated returns.
concepts.where_it_differs: The three-derivatives model emphasizes *architectural convergence and dominant-design lock-in* rather than capital cycle mechanics or financial dynamics. It is more about *technology and competition* and less about *money, credit, and investor behavior*. The lag between value creation and value capture is partially explained by time to reach inflection, not just by supply-demand cycles.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous Capital Goods (Austrian Capital Structure)
concepts.definition: Capital goods are highly specific to their current use and cannot be instantly redirected or liquidated into alternative production. A railway track, fiber-optic cable, or factory assembly line cannot be easily converted to other sectors. Changes in the structure of production (from hand-crafted to assembly-line, or from on-premise to cloud computing) cannot be quickly reversed. This heterogeneity means that when malinvestment is revealed, the capital goods remain (stranded capacity) and recovery requires waiting for demand to catch up or finding new uses.
concepts.originator: Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, Hayek; central to Austrian capital theory
concepts.canonical_source: Austrian Economics texts on capital structure; Hayek's The Pure Theory of Capital
concepts.what_it_captures: Why Phase 2 overcapacity *persists*—capital goods can't instantly disappear or be repurposed. The 20-50 year lag between malinvestment bust and productive use is partly because you must wait for technological and demand shifts that make the stranded capacity valuable again. For railways, it took decades for population to grow to use all the 'redundant' tracks; for fiber, it took cloud computing and streaming; for AI data centers, it will take breakthrough use cases.
concepts.where_it_differs: This is an explanation of *why* the lag is long and *why* idle infrastructure persists, not an explanation of the capital cycle itself. It's structural and technological; it doesn't explain the role of credit expansion or why capital flows in the first place.

concepts.name: Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (Installation/Deployment Periods)
concepts.definition: Carlota Perez's framework dividing technological revolutions into two periods: Installation (irruption and frenzy phases with speculative capital and new technology emergence) and Deployment (synergy and maturity phases with profitability and spreading through economy). Financial capital drives irruption/frenzy; production capital dominates synergy/maturity.
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Pérez, 'Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital: The Dynamics of Bubbles and Golden Ages' (2002)
concepts.originator: Carlota Pérez, 1990s-2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: All three layers: primary invention (irruption), forced reorganization via financial bubble creating overcapacity (frenzy), enablement of new industries (synergy/maturity)
concepts.where_it_differs: Perez emphasizes the financial-productive capital cycle rather than value capture distribution across winners; focuses on paradigm-level shifts spanning 50-70 years

concepts.name: Productive Bubbles
concepts.definition: Bill Janeway's concept that financial bubbles—despite their destructive crashes—leave behind valuable infrastructure and capability that enables a following generation of productive applications. State investment and guarantor role accelerates this process.
concepts.canonical_source: Bill Janeway, 'Doing Capitalism in the Innovation Economy: Markets, Speculation and the State' (2012)
concepts.originator: William H. Janeway, venture capitalist and economist, 2000s-2010s
concepts.what_it_captures: The 2nd-order bubble/overcapacity building physical and organizational capacity; the 3rd-order use of that stranded infrastructure by different businesses
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not emphasize the primary innovation itself; focuses on bubbles as economically productive despite losses; emphasizes state's role in de-risking early phases

concepts.name: Kondratieff/Kondratiev Long Waves
concepts.definition: Long-term economic cycles lasting 50-60 years, driven by clusters of technological innovations that reshape production and demand. Alternating upward (expansion) and downward (contraction) phases, each wave built on new core technologies (steam, railways, electricity, chemicals, ICT).
concepts.canonical_source: Nikolai Kondratieff (1920s-1930s); developed further by Schumpeter and contemporary long-wave theorists
concepts.originator: Nikolai Kondratieff, Russian economist, 1920s
concepts.what_it_captures: The multi-decade cycle of innovation waves; the alternation between growth and crisis phases that enable sectoral reorganization
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not explicitly address value capture distribution or how one group's infrastructure becomes another's platform; less emphasis on financial mechanisms

concepts.name: Creative Destruction
concepts.definition: Joseph Schumpeter's concept that capitalism progresses through waves of innovation where new technologies and business methods replace old ones, with entrepreneurs driving business cycles through clusters of simultaneous innovations. The process is both destructive (obsoleting old ways) and creative (enabling new possibilities).
concepts.canonical_source: Joseph Schumpeter, 'Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy' (1942); extended in trade cycle theory
concepts.originator: Joseph Schumpeter, Austrian economist, 1930s-1940s
concepts.what_it_captures: The forced reorganization of economic structure; the cyclical emergence of waves; the destruction-enabling paradox
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on competition and displacement rather than infrastructure accumulation; does not address the long lag between layers or value migration to different beneficiaries

concepts.name: General Purpose Technology (GPT)
concepts.definition: A technology with broad applicability across many industries, characterized by significant cross-sectoral spillovers, ongoing technological improvement, and cascading complementary innovations. Creates externalities and productivity growth as other industries adapt and build upon it.
concepts.canonical_source: Developed by economists studying electricity, computing, IT; recent AI applications. Ericsson, CEPR, NBER work on technology diffusion
concepts.originator: Emerged from growth economics literature, 1990s-2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: The enabling platform nature of layer 1; the cascading waves of downstream innovation; knowledge spillovers creating value for later entrants
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not explicitly model the 2nd-order reorganization/overcapacity phase or the lag; focuses on positive productivity spillovers rather than waste or malinvestment

concepts.name: Installation Period (Perez framework)
concepts.definition: In Perez's model, the first 20-30 years of a technological revolution characterized by irruption (new technology emerges, attracts ventures and speculative capital) followed by frenzy (bubble-like competition for adjacent applications, unsustainable debt, malinvestment). Creates infrastructure surplus.
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Pérez, 'Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital' (2002)
concepts.originator: Carlota Pérez, 2002
concepts.what_it_captures: Layers 1 and 2: primary innovation and forced reorganization via speculative overcapacity
concepts.where_it_differs: Half of Perez's two-period model; does not alone address value capture in the third layer

concepts.name: Deployment Period (Perez framework)
concepts.definition: In Perez's model, the second 20-30 years of a technological revolution, beginning after a 'golden age' or systemic reset, characterized by synergy (large firms dominate, standards and reliability emphasized over innovation) and maturity (technology becomes routine, diffuses throughout economy, new opportunities for investment decline). Stranded infrastructure becomes productive foundation.
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Pérez, 'Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital' (2002)
concepts.originator: Carlota Pérez, 2002
concepts.what_it_captures: Layer 3: a different set of winners capturing value by building on the now-cheap infrastructure and standardized platform from layer 2
concepts.where_it_differs: Second half of Perez's model; emphasizes standardization and diffusion rather than disruption or new business models

concepts.name: Dark Fiber
concepts.definition: Fiber optic cables laid during speculative booms (dot-com bubble, telecom build-out) but left unused because demand did not materialize at projected levels. Later re-lit and repurposed by cloud providers and content platforms at pennies on the dollar, becoming foundational infrastructure for modern internet services.
concepts.canonical_source: Contemporary tech history; examined in case studies of telecom overbuilding (1990s-2000s)
concepts.originator: Industry term, emerged ~2000s as metaphor for stranded but valuable infrastructure
concepts.what_it_captures: The mechanism by which 2nd-order overcapacity becomes 3rd-order enabler; the temporal lag and value inversion
concepts.where_it_differs: Specific infrastructure example rather than general framework; does not address organizational reorganization or business model innovation

concepts.name: Increasing Returns and Path Dependence
concepts.definition: W. Brian Arthur's model showing that technologies subject to increasing returns (where adoption costs fall with use or network value rises) can become locked-in through small historical accidents. Systems can lock into suboptimal technologies due to network effects, and initial choices constrain future development.
concepts.canonical_source: W. Brian Arthur, 'Increasing Returns and Path Dependence in the Economy' (1994); seminal paper 'Competing Technologies, Increasing Returns, and Lock-In by Historical Events' (1989)
concepts.originator: W. Brian Arthur, economist, 1980s-1990s
concepts.what_it_captures: The mechanism by which infrastructure and standards in layer 2 constrain and enable layer 3; why historical accidents in early adoption shape future winners
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on equilibrium selection and lock-in rather than value distribution or the productive role of overcapacity; does not address the lag or different beneficiary groups

concepts.name: Disruptive Innovation
concepts.definition: Clayton Christensen's theory that new technologies often enter at the market's bottom (low-cost, targeted at non-consumption), initially seem inferior to incumbents' offerings, but gradually move upmarket, displacing established players. Disruptors typically succeed when incumbents rationally ignore them.
concepts.canonical_source: Clayton Christensen, 'The Innovator's Dilemma' (1997); extended in subsequent works
concepts.originator: Clayton Christensen, Harvard Business School, 1990s
concepts.what_it_captures: The displacement of layer 1 by layer 3 businesses; the underestimation by incumbents of new opportunities on re-organized infrastructure
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on market displacement and business model innovation rather than infrastructure accumulation or forced reorganization; does not address the lag or the productive role of overcapacity

concepts.name: Value Migration
concepts.definition: In Christensen's framework, value systematically shifts within and between industries as technology architectures change. Profit concentrates where competitive advantages are defensible at any given time, and as modularity increases, value migrates from components to system-level aggregation.
concepts.canonical_source: Clayton Christensen, 'The Innovator's Dilemma' and subsequent works on modularity and value networks
concepts.originator: Clayton Christensen, 1990s-2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: The temporal lag in value capture; how layer 2 infrastructure becomes layer 3 enabler; how different groups benefit at different times
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes value movement but not the underlying infrastructure/reorganization mechanism; less emphasis on overcapacity or bubbles

concepts.name: Techno-Economic Paradigm Shift (Perez)
concepts.definition: Broader concept than single technologies: a shift in the dominant technological paradigm affecting how production is organized economy-wide. Includes changes in infrastructure, production methods, skill requirements, and organizational forms. Enables a new set of industries and business models suited to the new paradigm.
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Pérez, 'Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital' (2002)
concepts.originator: Carlota Pérez, 1990s-2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: The systematic reorganization (layer 2) that enables new possibilities (layer 3); the paradigm-level scope of change
concepts.where_it_differs: Broader and less specific than the 3-layer model; emphasizes institutional change rather than value capture dynamics

concepts.name: Great Surges of Development (Perez)
concepts.definition: Perez's term for major waves of technological revolution and diffusion spanning centuries, each surge including multiple technological revolutions. Each surge produces a cohort of countries that enter it early (gaining advantage) and those that enter later (facing installed paradigms and lock-in).
concepts.canonical_source: Carlota Pérez, various works and lectures; extended in 'Financing Innovation to Grow: New Challenges and Appropriate Tools' (2010s)
concepts.originator: Carlota Pérez, 2000s onwards
concepts.what_it_captures: The long-term lag and multi-generational nature; how early layers build infrastructure that constrains later entrants; the institutional learning process
concepts.where_it_differs: Development-focused; emphasizes geographic and institutional dimensions rather than value distribution among business actors

concepts.name: Socio-Technical Transitions
concepts.definition: Multi-dimensional change involving simultaneous shifts in technology, social practices, regulations, cultural norms, supply chains, and institutions. Transitions involve stability-lock mechanisms (formal rules, informal norms, vested interests) that resist change, but eventually new regimes establish themselves with new lock-in patterns.
concepts.canonical_source: Frank Geels and others in sustainability transitions literature; applied to various technology shifts
concepts.originator: Frank Geels, Marko Hekkert, 2000s onwards
concepts.what_it_captures: The forced reorganization (layer 2) of society, not just technology; the institutional and regulatory changes enabling layer 3
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not specifically address value capture or financial dynamics; emphasizes regulatory and social resistance rather than bubbles or overcapacity

concepts.name: Productivity Slowdown and Technology Absorption
concepts.definition: Phenomenon where major innovations show productivity impacts with significant lags (5-20 years), as organizations reorganize, workforce trains, and complementary systems mature. Early investments in technology may not show returns until supporting infrastructure and capabilities develop.
concepts.canonical_source: Solow productivity paradox; Erik Brynjolfsson, Andrew McAfee work on technology productivity gaps
concepts.originator: Observed in 1980s-1990s computing; formalized by Brynjolfsson, McAfee, 2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: The lag between layer 1 (technology invention) and layer 3 (value realization); the reorganization burden
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on productivity measurement rather than value distribution; does not address overcapacity or infrastructure building

concepts.name: Gartner Hype Cycle
concepts.definition: Five-stage model (technology trigger → peak of inflated expectations → trough of disillusionment → slope of enlightenment → plateau of productivity) combining hype levels (bell curve) with technological maturity (S-curve). The trough is characterized by investment write-offs and failed implementations.
concepts.canonical_source: Gartner research methodology, established ~2000s
concepts.originator: Gartner, Inc., early 2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: Layer 2 overcapacity and malinvestment (trough of disillusionment); the transition to productive use (slope of enlightenment to plateau)
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes adoption psychology and maturity curves but not the economic value distribution or the enabling infrastructure dynamics

concepts.name: Infrastructure Paradox
concepts.definition: Challenge that complementary infrastructure layers (spectrum, backhaul, data centers, power grids) are governed separately but depend on each other, creating timing mismatches. Overbuilding one layer strands capacity; underbuilding creates bottlenecks. Historical cycle: overbuild now and risk stranded assets, or wait and risk lock-out by competitors.
concepts.canonical_source: Contemporary infrastructure studies; extensively discussed in AI infrastructure investment debates, 2024-2026
concepts.originator: Wesley Whited, Alok Agrawal, and infrastructure economics, 2020s
concepts.what_it_captures: The 2nd-order overcapacity problem; the coordination failures that create waste; the later re-purposing of stranded infrastructure
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on coordinating failures rather than the productive value capture of layer 3; does not address business model innovation

concepts.name: Network Effects and Cumulative Causation
concepts.definition: Technologies exhibiting network effects increase in value as more users adopt them, creating positive feedback loops and threshold effects (critical mass). Adoption accelerates exponentially once critical mass is reached, locking in early choices and creating winner-take-most dynamics.
concepts.canonical_source: Network economics literature; relevant to infrastructure buildout and platform effects
concepts.originator: Katz & Shapiro, 1980s-1990s; extended in network science
concepts.what_it_captures: The mechanism by which layer 2 infrastructure becomes layer 3 enabling platform; self-reinforcing adoption cycles
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes adoption dynamics but not value distribution across different beneficiary groups; does not address the lag or malinvestment

concepts.name: Paradigm Shift (Kuhn)
concepts.discipline: Philosophy of science / Science and technology studies
concepts.definition: Thomas Kuhn's theory that science (and by extension, technology) progresses through revolutionary shifts where fundamental frameworks and assumptions change. Shifts occur when existing paradigms accumulate anomalies, prompting crisis and revolution leading to new normal science under a new paradigm.
concepts.canonical_source: Thomas Kuhn, 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962); applied to technology in later works
concepts.originator: Thomas Kuhn, philosopher of science, 1960s
concepts.what_it_captures: The revolutionary, system-wide nature of layer 1 innovation; the institutional and conceptual reorganization (layer 2)
concepts.where_it_differs: Philosophy of knowledge rather than economics; does not address value capture, financial dynamics, or the lag

concepts.name: Overbuilding (in infrastructure cycles)
concepts.definition: Historical pattern where optimism about a transformative technology (railways, telegraphy, electricity, fiber optics, AI compute) drives speculative investment in infrastructure far exceeding immediate demand, resulting in stranded capacity, financial losses, and eventual value realization when demand catches up or technology matures.
concepts.canonical_source: Historical case studies: UK railway mania (1840s), telecom bubble (1990s), discussed in 'Overbuilding the Future' and infrastructure analyses
concepts.originator: Observed cyclically in economic history; formalized in contemporary analyses
concepts.what_it_captures: Layer 2 malinvestment and overcapacity; the 20-50 year lag until stranded infrastructure becomes productive
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes the waste but not the organizational reorganization or how value is captured by layer 3 beneficiaries

concepts.name: Knowledge Spillovers and Positive Externalities
concepts.definition: Unintended spread of technological knowledge and capabilities from one firm, region, or sector to others, creating positive externalities where social benefits exceed private returns to the original innovator. Spillovers travel via worker mobility, imitation, collaboration, and industry networks.
concepts.canonical_source: Endogenous growth theory; CEPR, NBER research on technology diffusion
concepts.originator: Developed in growth economics, 1990s-2000s
concepts.what_it_captures: The mechanism by which layer 1 innovation enables layer 3 beneficiaries; the value creation beyond the original innovator
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on knowledge diffusion rather than infrastructure; does not address the organizational reorganization or lag

concepts.name: Cascading Innovation
concepts.definition: Process where major innovations create market size effects that incentivize complementary innovations both upstream and downstream. Breakthrough in one layer increases demand for adjacent layers, spurring innovation that multiplies the impact of the original technology.
concepts.canonical_source: Carvalho & Draca, 'Cascading Innovation' (2017); ScienceDirect research on complementary technology ecosystems
concepts.originator: Carvalho & Draca, economics of innovation, 2010s
concepts.what_it_captures: The multiplication effect of layer 1 enabling cascades of layer 3 innovations; how a single primary innovation spawns generations
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on downstream innovation effects rather than reorganization or value capture dynamics

concepts.name: Technological Trajectory
concepts.definition: The path that innovation in a particular technology area follows over time. Trajectories have momentum and can get locked-in through institutionalization of ideas, markets, and professions. Development follows both scientific advance and economic/institutional factors, until saturation is reached.
concepts.canonical_source: Technology management and innovation literature; ScienceDirect, MIT Sloan
concepts.originator: Dosi, others in evolutionary economics, 1980s-1990s
concepts.what_it_captures: The path-dependent nature of technology development; how layer 2 choices constrain layer 3 possibilities
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes technology evolution but not value distribution or the lag; does not address business model changes

concepts.name: Platform and Layer Architecture (infrastructure stacking)
concepts.definition: View of technology as layered (energy/compute/frameworks/platforms/applications), where each layer provides foundation for the layer above. Innovation and value migration flow through shifts in which layer is constraining; infrastructure layers create platform constraints/opportunities for application layers.
concepts.canonical_source: Madrona Ventures, Medium articles on AI infrastructure; contemporary platform architecture discussions
concepts.originator: Contemporary platform economy analysis, 2020s
