concepts.what_it_captures: The multi-layer nature of technology systems; how layer 2 infrastructure enables layer 3 applications; bottleneck-driven value capture
concepts.where_it_differs: Describes layered architecture but not the temporal lag or financial/bubble dynamics; treats layers as simultaneous rather than sequential

concepts.name: Venture Capital Funding Waves
concepts.definition: Capital markets exhibit boom-bust cycles where speculative capital floods into high-growth sectors (dotcom, biotech, AI), driving up valuations and infrastructure investment, followed by crashes that leave behind ecosystem development, capabilities, and infrastructure enabling later companies. Capital availability cycles independently from technology maturity.
concepts.canonical_source: Kevin Siskar 'Booms, Busts, and Billion-Dollar Breakthroughs'; contemporary VC analysis
concepts.originator: Observed empirically in VC markets; formalized in contemporary analyses
concepts.what_it_captures: Layer 2 overcapacity driven by financial cycles; how bubbles fund infrastructure; value capturing layer 3 benefits from layer 2 wreckage
concepts.where_it_differs: Focuses on capital availability cycles rather than technology reorganization; does not specifically address organizational changes

concepts.name: Financial Instability Hypothesis (Minsky)
concepts.definition: Hyman Minsky's theory that prolonged stability breeds instability through endogenous growth of leverage and speculation. Firms cycle through hedge (stable) finance to speculative to Ponzi finance, creating boom conditions. Financial crises are inevitable outcomes, not exogenous shocks, leaving infrastructure and capabilities behind.
concepts.canonical_source: Hyman Minsky, 'Stabilizing an Unstable Economy' (1986); developed through 1990s
concepts.originator: Hyman Minsky, Keynesian economist, 1970s-1990s
concepts.what_it_captures: The financial bubble mechanism (layer 2); how stability-induced over-leverage creates infrastructure; boom-bust cycle leaving capacity behind
concepts.where_it_differs: Financial rather than technological focus; does not address organizational reorganization or how layer 3 captures value

concepts.name: Fourth Industrial Revolution / Industry 4.0
concepts.definition: Contemporary framing of major technological shifts (First: steam/mechanical; Second: electricity; Third: computing/digital; Fourth: cyber-physical systems/IoT/AI) as historically ordered waves. Each wave forces reorganization of production, labor, and society.
concepts.canonical_source: Klaus Schwab 'The Fourth Industrial Revolution' (2016); contemporary technology adoption literature
concepts.originator: Klaus Schwab, World Economic Forum, 2016
concepts.what_it_captures: The multi-wave nature of technology history; the forced reorganization at each transition; the generational lag between waves
concepts.where_it_differs: Descriptive of technology waves rather than mechanisms; does not address value capture or bubble dynamics

concepts.name: Enabling Technology
concepts.definition: Technology that enhances capabilities of users or organizations and can be applied across diverse fields. Acts as foundation for further advancements, with impact multiplied through complementary innovations. Enables uses that were previously impossible or economically infeasible.
concepts.canonical_source: Technology and innovation literature; applies to electricity, computing, internet infrastructure
concepts.originator: Technology studies, used throughout 20th-21st centuries
concepts.what_it_captures: Layer 1 primary innovation; the enabling property that makes layer 3 possible; the platform nature
concepts.where_it_differs: Does not address the reorganization (layer 2) or the lag in value capture; focuses on capability expansion rather than value distribution

cases.name: Telegraph Network
cases.primary: Invention of electrical telegraph (Morse, Cooke & Wheatstone, 1830s-1840s) enabling instant long-distance communication
cases.secondary: Massive overbuild of competing telegraph networks: 75+ companies by 1851 operating overlapping, redundant routes across North America and Britain; network congestion and poor service quality from duplication
third_order: Modern financial markets with price discovery
Arbitrage elimination and information-symmetric trading
Real-time transmission of stock prices enabling broad public participation
cases.transmission_mechanism: Instant price transmission destroyed the information asymmetry that had enriched middlemen and arbitrageurs for centuries. By enabling identical price quotes across cities simultaneously, telegraph networks transformed stock and commodity exchanges from bilateral negotiation markets into centralized, transparent price-discovery mechanisms. The Stock Exchange became the largest telegraph consumer, with half of London's telegraph traffic by 1850s being stock-market data.
cases.who_captured_value: Financial institutions and traders in cities with direct telegraph access (London, New York, Chicago); not the telegraph inventors or early companies (most failed or were consolidated)
cases.lag_years: 20-30 years (overcapacity 1840s-1850s; financial market transformation visible 1860s-1870s; Panic of 1857 first crisis to spread via telegraph)
cases.fourth_order: Ticker tape machines (1867+) and later electronic trading infrastructure
cases.counterfactual: Without telegraph overcapacity, financial markets would have remained local and fragmented. Stock exchanges in different cities would have operated on delayed, imperfect price information for decades longer, delaying the emergence of modern portfolio trading and risk management.

cases.name: British Railway Mania
cases.primary: Development of steam-powered railway technology (locomotives, track, switching systems enabling long-distance transport)
cases.secondary: Speculative bubble and massive overcapacity: 1846 alone saw 263 Parliamentary acts authorizing 9,500 miles of new railways with £132 million capital (45% of total domestic investment that year). By 1847, railway investment exceeded £30m annually. Nearly one-third of authorized lines were never built; shareholders suffered 50% losses between 1846-1850.
third_order: Standardized time zones (forced adoption for operational scheduling)
Nationalization of communication standards
Foundation for later continental transport integration
cases.transmission_mechanism: The overcapacity of redundant rail lines created an operational coordination crisis: trains running between cities discovered they could not maintain timetables because each company and city operated on local time. This forced railways to adopt 'Railway Time' (1840s in Britain), which eventually led to the standardized time zones adopted globally (Greenwich Meridian 1884). The need to physically coordinate thousands of trains and stations made time standardization operationally mandatory, not voluntary.
cases.who_captured_value: Not the railway investors (most lost money) or companies (many failed), but businesses that depended on precise scheduling: telegraphers, shipping companies, financial markets, and later manufacturing and logistics firms.
cases.lag_years: 40-45 years (bubble 1846; time standardization visible 1850s-1870s; formalized 1883-1884)
cases.counterfactual: Without railway mania's overcapacity creating operational chaos, time standardization would likely have been delayed another 30+ years. Local solar time would have persisted in most cities, making coordinated transport and communication impossible at scale.

cases.name: US Railway Expansion & Overbuilding
cases.primary: Expansion and refinement of railway technology and continental rail network (post-Civil War reconstruction and western expansion)
cases.secondary: Massive speculative overbuilding: redundant competing lines, unsustainable debt-financed expansion, repeated cycles of boom and bust (particularly 1873 panic). Overexpansion created underutilized rail capacity, destroyed returns on capital for investors, bankrupted many operators.
third_order: Mail-order retail giants (Sears founded 1893, Montgomery Ward 1872) exploiting cheap, reliable freight service
Commodity futures markets (Chicago Board of Trade, standardized contracts 1865+, modern clearing by 1880s)
National brand retailers via railroads
Standardized time zones (Nov 18, 1883)
Chicago as commodity hub with standardized grain grading
cases.transmission_mechanism: The overcapacity of rail freight service created unprofitably cheap rates for small-package shipping. Sears exploited this by printing massive catalogs and delivering via freight railways to rural customers nationwide—a business model impossible before railways had excess capacity seeking any revenue. Commodity trading similarly depended on reliable overnight grain shipment between regional markets; the overbuilt rail network made this feasible. Standardized time zones (forced by operational needs of multiple competing rail companies) enabled coordinated national supply chains.
cases.who_captured_value: Mail-order retailers (Sears, Montgomery Ward, later catalog companies), commodity traders, farmers gaining direct market access, financial markets. Not the railway companies (most investors lost money).
cases.lag_years: 15-20 years (overbuilding 1870s-1880s; mail order scaling 1890s+; commodity standardization in place by 1880s)
cases.counterfactual: Without railway overcapacity, freight rates would have remained high, making mail-order retail unviable (cost of shipping outweighed margins). Commodity trading would have remained local. Continental time standardization would have been delayed decades. National retail chains could not have emerged.

cases.name: Bessemer Steel Process
cases.primary: Invention of Bessemer process for mass-producing steel (1856), enabling bulk manufacturing of high-quality steel at scale
cases.secondary: Massive buildup of steel production capacity; dramatic cost reductions: from £50-60 per ton (1850s) to £6-7 per ton (1870s), then to $18-32 per ton by 1890s in US. Annual US Bessemer-steel rail production: 2,550 tons (1867, $170/ton) → 1.5 million tons (1884, $32/ton).
third_order: Affordable railroad rail enabling continental rail expansion
Long-span bridge construction (previously limited by iron)
Steel-frame building construction enabling skyscrapers
Naval armor plating and modern warship construction
cases.transmission_mechanism: The cost reduction crossed critical thresholds, making previously uneconomical infrastructure projects viable. Steel rails became cheap enough to justify laying track in less-trafficked routes; bridges could now span distances previously requiring multiple spans; buildings could rise vertically with steel frames. Each required not just cheaper steel, but steel cheap ENOUGH that engineers could justify the investment in new categories of infrastructure.
cases.who_captured_value: Railroad operators, construction companies, city developers, governments building national infrastructure. Not Bessemer (he sold his patents) or early steel companies (marginal returns in competitive market).
cases.lag_years: 15-20 years (process 1856; cost floor hit by early 1870s enabling mass infrastructure)
cases.counterfactual: Without Bessemer overcapacity cost reduction, steel would have remained luxury material for specialized uses. Rail networks would have remained sparse, bridges small, skyscrapers impossible. Infrastructure development delayed 20-30 years; landscape of cities fundamentally different.

cases.name: Printing Press
cases.primary: Invention of Gutenberg's movable-type printing press (~1450) enabling mechanical reproduction of texts
cases.secondary: Explosive proliferation of printing: ~30,000 books in all of Europe pre-1450; 10-20 million printed books by 1500. 250+ cities had printing presses by 1500. By 1600, printed materials had become dominant information medium. This was overcapacity relative to demand—many printers competed, many ventures failed, but infrastructure persisted.
third_order: Scientific Revolution (1550s-1700s)
Standardized knowledge bases enabling cumulative science
Reformation and religious pluralism
Modern university system
Reproducible empirical investigation
cases.transmission_mechanism: Manuscript culture prevented science because copied texts drifted—each copy accumulated errors, variations, and marginal notes. Printed texts guaranteed 'typographical fixity': all copies identical. This allowed scientists across Europe to reference the SAME diagrams, observations, and data without suspicion of transcription error. Cumulative knowledge-building became possible; standardized visual representations (anatomical plates, maps, botanical drawings) created shared visual language. Without identical texts, the scientific community and reproducible methodology could not have emerged.
cases.who_captured_value: Scientists, universities, Protestant reformers, merchants (printed business forms, contracts, standardized ledgers), nation-states (standardized laws, regulations). Not Gutenberg (died moderately wealthy but not rich) or early printers (highly competitive, low margins).
cases.lag_years: 100-150 years (printing 1450s; scientific revolution proper 1550s-1600s; full impact on knowledge production 1600s-1700s)
cases.counterfactual: Without printing press overcapacity and standardization, the scientific revolution could not have occurred. Science fundamentally depends on reproducible, cumulative knowledge. Handwriting culture prevented this. Enlightenment, industrial revolution, modernity itself depend on printing-enabled science.

cases.name: Dutch Fluyt Ship & Amsterdam Entrepôt
cases.primary: Design innovation in cargo ships: the fluyt (~1580s-1590s) with pear-shaped hull, flat bottom, shallow draft, large cargo hold (200-600 tons), requiring only 12-20 crew vs. 40-60 for earlier types
cases.secondary: Massive adoption creating overcapacity of shipping: By 1660s, Dutch Republic operated 1,500-2,000 fluyts and controlled ~50% of European shipping tonnage. Shipping costs collapsed; competition intensified among Dutch shippers.
third_order: Dutch East India Company (VOC, founded 1602) monopoly on Asian spice trade
Amsterdam as global financial capital and entrepôt
Modern joint-stock company and investment markets (VOC was first publicly-traded company)
Global supply chains for luxury goods
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cost reduction in shipping (per-ton-mile) crossed the threshold where it became economically viable for Dutch merchants to attempt to monopolize long-distance trade to Asia and control bulk commodity flows (Baltic grain, salt, etc.). The fluyt's efficiency allowed Dutch to undercut competitors' prices, dominate European bulk trades, and establish Amsterdam as the clearing house for European commerce. The enormous wealth flowing through Amsterdam then enabled investment in the VOC and the financial innovations that followed.
cases.who_captured_value: Dutch merchants, Amsterdam trading companies, VOC investors (first modern stock market), Dutch state (via taxation and military power). Not ship designers or early fluyt operators (competed away).
cases.lag_years: 20-25 years (fluyt innovation 1580s-1590s; Dutch shipping dominance visible 1610s-1620s; VOC established 1602)
cases.counterfactual: Without fluyt cost reduction, Dutch could not have dominated European shipping or established monopolistic control of Asian trade routes. VOC would not have been founded, or would have been English/Portuguese initiative instead. Amsterdam would not have become financial capital. Global trade integration delayed.

cases.name: British Canal Mania
cases.primary: Development of canal-lock technology and civil engineering techniques enabling artificial waterways to transport bulk goods
cases.secondary: Speculative bubble: 1791-1794 saw 80+ canal acts approved; massive capital investment; construction costs exceeded expectations; toll revenues lagged; competition between overlapping routes eroded returns. Investors lost heavily; many canals profitable only on optimistic projections.
third_order: Infrastructure template for railways (engineering, route planning, land acquisition, corporate structures)
Trained civil engineers and laborers for railway construction
Canal capital partly recycled into railway investment (1830s-1840s)
cases.transmission_mechanism: Canal mania trained a generation of civil engineers in large-scale infrastructure projects. When railways emerged as superior technology, the same engineers, labor forces, corporate governance structures, and route-planning experience transferred directly to rail construction. Canal investors, facing obsolescence, recycled capital into railway companies. The canal-era 'railway bill' legislative template became the model for 1840s railway mania.
cases.who_captured_value: Railway companies, civil engineers (whose skills transferred), later railway investors. Not canal investors (most lost money).
cases.lag_years: 40-50 years (canal mania 1790s-1810s; railways emerge 1830s; railways clearly dominant 1840s-1860s)
cases.counterfactual: Without canal mania's infrastructure bubble, the 1840s railway mania might have been smaller and slower. Britain would not have had a trained corps of large-scale infrastructure engineers, land agents, and corporate structures ready to build railways. Railway expansion would have faced greater technical and organizational learning costs.

cases.name: Factory Electrification
cases.primary: Electric motor and generator technology becoming economically viable for factory use, replacing steam-driven line-shaft systems
cases.secondary: Factory reorganization forced by new power distribution: physical rebuilding of factory floors from centralized steam-engine architecture (with belt-driven line shafts transmitting power) to distributed electric motor architecture requiring complete spatial reconfiguration
third_order: Assembly-line mass production systems (continuous-flow manufacturing)
Cheap mass-produced goods (automobiles, appliances)
Manufacturing abundance and standardization of consumer products
Military-industrial production capacity (WWII)
cases.transmission_mechanism: Electric power eliminated the mechanical constraints of line-shaft systems, requiring factories to be physically rebuilt. This reorganization enabled continuous-flow production geometries that made assembly-line manufacturing economically viable and necessary. Factory reorganization was the enabling lever.
cases.who_captured_value: Automobile manufacturers (Ford, GM) and assembly-line operators; not electricity generators or motor manufacturers. Consumers benefited via cheaper goods but did not capture the economic value.
cases.lag_years: 20-40 years (tertiary becomes visible 1920s-1940s)
cases.counterfactual: Without the factory reorganization forced by electric motors, the spatial and temporal reconfigurations required for assembly-line mass production would not have been economically viable or organizationally necessary. The primary innovation could have diffused without triggering the second-order change.
cases.fourth_order: Military-industrial capacity and WWII mass production (operator's example)

cases.name: Containerization
cases.primary: Standardized shipping container and purpose-built containership design (Malcolm McLean, Ideal-X first voyage April 1956)
cases.secondary: Port infrastructure overhaul and stranded assets: widespread investment in container-capable ports, rendering older ports (London, etc.) economically obsolete; labor displacement (dockworker numbers halved); stranded manual cargo-handling infrastructure; labor union resistance to automation
third_order: Global supply chains and intermodal transport networks
Just-in-time manufacturing and distributed inventory
Offshore manufacturing and outsourcing
E-commerce logistics infrastructure (Amazon distribution model)
cases.transmission_mechanism: Container standardization created intermodal seamlessness (container fits ship-truck-rail-port sequences identically), solving coordination problems. Port infrastructure overbuild freed capital and real estate; labor displacement released capital. Cost collapse from $5.83/ton to $0.16/ton (97% reduction) crossed a threshold enabling new business models based on distributed, rapid inventory cycles.
cases.who_captured_value: Retailers (Walmart, Amazon), global e-commerce platforms, offshore manufacturers. Not shipping companies or port operators (who faced margin compression).
cases.lag_years: 15-20 years (tertiary becomes visible 1970s-1990s)
cases.counterfactual: Without containerization's infrastructure overbuild and labor displacement, the distributed supply-chain model enabling Amazon and Walmart's logistics networks (which require rapid, low-cost intermodal cycles) would not have been economically viable.
cases.fourth_order: Global trade liberalization and manufacturing location arbitrage

cases.name: Interstate Highway System
cases.primary: Federal Highway Act (1956) authorizing 41,000 miles of standardized, high-capacity interstate highways, initially budgeted at $25 billion (approximately $500 billion in 2016 dollars)
cases.secondary: Massive infrastructure overbuild: stranded railroad assets (branch lines, rail yards, freight terminals became economically obsolete); old transportation routes rendered irrelevant; public capital crowding out private rail investment; disruption of existing regional trade patterns centered on rail hubs
third_order: Logistics economy and trucking networks
Just-in-time manufacturing supply chains
Suburban development and decentralized retail
E-commerce distribution centers (Walmart hub-and-spoke model)
cases.transmission_mechanism: Standardized highway network created a physical infrastructure enabling distributed logistics previously impossible via rail. Stranded railroad assets (capital sunk in unprofitable branch lines) became worthless, freeing capital and real estate. Public financing of highways (via federal gas tax) while railroads self-financed created cost-structure shift enabling truck-based logistics. Returns of $6-$1.80 per $1 invested suggest third-order value creation was enormous.
cases.who_captured_value: Trucking industry operators, retailers (Walmart's distribution efficiency exploited highway density), suburban developers, e-commerce platforms. Not highway users or general public.
cases.lag_years: 15-30 years (tertiary becomes visible 1970s-1980s with Walmart distribution innovation)
cases.counterfactual: Without the stranded railroad infrastructure and the shift to truck-based logistics enabled by highway density, Walmart's distributed supply-chain model (which requires rapid, flexible trucking) would not have been economically viable. Regional retail would have remained concentrated near rail hubs.
cases.fourth_order: Motorized logistics becoming dominant infrastructure, enabling e-commerce

cases.name: Apollo Program and Integrated Circuits
cases.primary: Apollo Guidance Computer specification requiring integrated circuits, establishing massive procurement demand for commercial ICs
cases.secondary: Massive IC overbuild: Apollo program consumed approximately 60% of world IC production (200,000+ circuits for AGC Block I testing alone); prices collapsed via manufacturing learning curve from $1000/unit (1960) to $25/unit (1963); Minuteman missile and Apollo together funded production improvements; overcapacity when Apollo budget peaked in mid-1960s
third_order: Minicomputers and personal computers (below cost threshold for viability)
Digital signal processing and consumer electronics
Semiconductor industry consolidation and vertical integration
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cost collapse below threshold ($25 instead of $1000) made entirely new applications economically viable. Manufacturing learning curve established by government procurement created predictable supply at sustainable costs. Overcapacity in IC manufacturing when Apollo spending peaked meant excess production capability absorbed into commercial markets.
cases.who_captured_value: PC manufacturers (Apple, IBM), consumer electronics companies, commercial semiconductor vendors. Not NASA or the defense department.
cases.lag_years: 10-20 years (tertiary becomes visible 1970s-1980s)
cases.counterfactual: Without the cost collapse and manufacturing capacity built by Apollo, the economic threshold for viable personal computers and consumer electronics would not have been crossed until 10-20 years later, if at all without alternative demand.
cases.fourth_order: Internet software industry enabled by affordable computing infrastructure

cases.name: Mechanical Refrigeration and Cold Chain
cases.primary: Reliable mechanical refrigeration technology replacing ice-based systems, enabling year-round temperature control
cases.secondary: Cold-chain infrastructure overbuild: 500+ large-scale cold storage facilities by early 1900s; 10 million tons annually stored by 1925; refrigerated rail cars and trucks; geographic decoupling of production from consumption creating geographic specialization pressure
third_order: Industrial agriculture and monoculture farming
Food processing and standardized commodity production
Supermarket chains and nationalized food supply
Regional agricultural specialization
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cold-chain infrastructure broke the seasonal and geographic constraints on food availability. This decoupling enabled large-scale industrial agriculture (production could exceed local consumption), which then required standardization, processing, and long-distance transport. The overbuild of cold infrastructure locked in industrial practices.
cases.who_captured_value: Food processing companies, supermarket chains and retailers (Kroger, A&P), logistics companies. Not cold-storage equipment manufacturers.
cases.lag_years: 20-40 years (tertiary becomes visible 1940s-1970s)
cases.counterfactual: Without the cold-chain infrastructure overbuild, industrial agriculture would not have been economically viable; agriculture would have remained seasonal, local, and based on preservation (salting, canning) rather than logistics.

cases.name: Green Revolution
cases.primary: High-yielding seed varieties, especially dwarf wheat developed at CIMMYT Mexico (Norman Borlaug, late 1950s), engineered to be highly responsive to fertilizer inputs
cases.secondary: Massive fertilizer and irrigation infrastructure overbuild: India imported 18,000 tons of Mexican seed (1966), triggering nationwide fertilizer and irrigation expansion; pesticide industry expansion; fixed-capital investment in farm equipment; agricultural extension systems; overproduction bubbles in some regions (stranded capital in irrigation projects in arid regions)
third_order: Industrial monoculture agriculture on massive scale
Biotechnology and seed industry consolidation
Global grain commodity markets and trade
Population growth and urbanization support
Feed-grain production for meat and dairy industries
cases.transmission_mechanism: HYV seeds were engineered to be responsive to chemical fertilizer (dwarf varieties concentrate energy into grain rather than stalk). This technical property created demand for fertilizer overbuild and irrigation expansion. The infrastructure overbuild locked in industrial agriculture practices; it made extensive cultivation and monoculture the only way to recoup capital. Global commodity markets emerged because industrial scale production enabled trade.
cases.who_captured_value: Seed companies, fertilizer manufacturers (Mosanto, Dow, etc.), grain traders, large mechanized farms. Not smallholder farmers or consumers (who got cheaper calories).
cases.lag_years: 10-20 years (tertiary becomes visible 1970s-1980s)
cases.counterfactual: Without the fertilizer/irrigation infrastructure overbuild driven by HYV seeds, industrial monoculture agriculture would not have been economically viable; agriculture would have remained diversified and smallholder-based.
cases.fourth_order: Agribusiness consolidation, genetic modification, agricultural trade liberalization

cases.name: Automobile Mass Production Assembly Line
cases.primary: Assembly-line mass production (Ford Motor Company 1914, moving conveyor system), reducing vehicle production time and cost (Model T price $850 to $275)
cases.secondary: Support-industry overcapacity and infrastructure overbuild: automobiles consumed 20% of US steel, 80% of rubber, 75% of plate glass production; road and gas-station infrastructure required; vertical integration at Ford (River Rouge complex by late 1920s); repair-shop and dealer networks; regional manufacturing clusters and employment disruption in non-automotive regions
third_order: Suburban development and decentralized real estate markets
Logistics and commercial vehicle networks
Military-industrial production systems (WWII)
Interstate commerce and goods distribution
cases.transmission_mechanism: Mass production required standardized, abundant parts supply, driving overcapacity in steel, rubber, glass industries. This encouraged vertical integration and multi-factory coordination systems. Standardization and modular design became template for logistics and later military production. Road infrastructure required by automobiles enabled suburban development (housing could be built at scale, distributed, served by private vehicles). Standardized assembly-line techniques were later directly applied to military manufacturing at scale.
cases.who_captured_value: Suburban real estate developers, logistics and commercial-vehicle operators, military-industrial contractors (WWII onwards). Not automobile buyers (who got cheaper cars).
cases.lag_years: 15-30 years (tertiary becomes visible 1930s-1940s, accelerating in WWII)
cases.counterfactual: Without the assembly-line infrastructure overbuild and supply-chain integration (especially the overcapacity in steel, rubber, glass and the standardization practices), neither suburban development at scale nor WWII military production at speed would have been feasible.
cases.fourth_order: Post-war motorized logistics dominance and suburbanization

cases.name: Semiconductor/Transistor Cost Collapse
cases.primary: Transistor (1947), integrated circuit (1958), microprocessor Intel 4004 (1971). Each fab process node generation produced exponential cost reductions through manufacturing scale and yield optimization.
cases.secondary: Massive semiconductor manufacturing buildout 1960s-1980s. Fab construction, process node shrinkage (10μ to 0.1μ), yield improvements. Cost per transistor: $10 (1960) → $1 (1970) → $0.01 (1980) → $0.001 (1990). Manufacturing capacity overcapacity cycles as demand fluctuated.
third_order: Personal computer industry (Apple II 1977, IBM PC 1981, Commodore 64 1982)
Software industry emergence (Lotus 1-2-3 1983, Excel, dBASE, WordPerfect)
Consumer electronics markets
Shift from mainframe-only to distributed computing
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cost threshold crossover. At $10/transistor: only governments and large corporations could build computers. At $0.001/transistor: computers became consumer appliances at ~$1000 price point. Without this cost collapse, PC markets never achieved scale sufficient for software industry viability.
cases.who_captured_value: Semiconductor manufacturers (Intel, AMD) captured some value. PC makers (IBM, Apple, Compaq) captured more. Software companies (Microsoft, Lotus) captured most sustainable long-term value. Original IC inventors (Kilby, Noyce) did not capture lasting competitive advantage.
cases.counterfactual: Without transistor cost collapse, computing would have remained restricted to institutions and military through 21st century. Personal computers, software industry, and consumer digital revolution would have been delayed decades or prevented.
sources: PC industry adoption timeline (Apple II 1977, IBM PC 1981)
Software company emergence dates (Lotus 1983, Microsoft Excel 1985)

cases.name: Barcode/UPC and Retail Data
cases.primary: UPC barcode standardization and retail adoption (1973-1974). First item scanned June 26, 1974 (Wrigley's gum, Troy, OH). Provided first real-time item-level sales data in retail sector.
cases.secondary: Massive retailer capex on point-of-sale terminals, barcode scanners, data networks (1974-1985). Organized retail (Kroger, Safeway, Walmart) adopted scanning infrastructure. Created stranded capex: invested scanners required data infrastructure to be leveraged to justify investment.
third_order: Supply chain optimization and category management 1990s onwards
Vendor-managed inventory (VMI) systems
Just-in-time retail distribution
Walmart EDLP (Everyday Low Price) dominance and logistics edge
Cross-dock distribution centers
cases.transmission_mechanism: Real-time item-level sales data enabled predictive inventory optimization. Pre-barcode: retailers had no demand visibility, replenishment was reactive. Post-barcode: visibility enabled inventory compression, stockout reduction, supplier term negotiation, shelf-space optimization. Data visibility became core competitive capability.
cases.who_captured_value: Walmart and efficient large retailers captured enormous value. Suppliers initially saw margin pressure, later learned VMI benefited them. Barcode equipment vendors (NCR) captured some value. Original UPC proponents did not sustain advantage.
cases.counterfactual: Without UPC barcodes providing item-level data, vendor-managed inventory, category management, and just-in-time retail would have been impossible. Walmart's competitive supply-chain advantage specifically derived from barcode-enabled data visibility.
sources: UPC first scan: June 26, 1974, Wrigley's gum, Troy, OH

cases.name: Military GPS Selective Availability Removal
cases.primary: GPS constellation developed by US military. First satellite 1978, fully operational 1995. System intentionally degraded for civilian use via Selective Availability, limiting civilian accuracy to ~100 meters.
cases.secondary: Consumer GPS receiver market development despite poor accuracy (1995-2000). Garmin, Magellan, TomTom invested in consumer GPS receivers for niche markets (surveying, aviation, recreation). Built infrastructure and supply chains constrained by accuracy limitations.
third_order: Location-based services and civilian location economy
Automotive GPS navigation (TomTom, Garmin car GPS)
Mobile location services (Google Maps, Waze, Uber, Lyft, DoorDash)
Location-enabled mobile applications (Pokemon GO, location APIs)
Ride-sharing and delivery economies
cases.transmission_mechanism: Accuracy threshold crossover at specific point. At 100m accuracy (SA enabled): GPS useless for driving. At 10-15m (SA disabled May 1, 2000): viable for automotive navigation. At <5m: pedestrian navigation and mobile gaming enabled. Selective Availability removal crossed multiple application viability thresholds.
cases.who_captured_value: Apple and Google captured most value via location platforms and APIs. Uber and Lyft captured ride-sharing value. Garmin/TomTom retained niche. DoD (system builder) did not capture commercial value.
cases.counterfactual: Without Selective Availability removal (policy decision required), civilian GPS would have remained niche. Mobile location services, ride-sharing, location-based social networks would have been delayed or prevented. The 10x accuracy improvement crossed critical application thresholds.

cases.name: Mobile Cellular Infrastructure Buildout
cases.primary: Cellular phone technology developed. First commercial: Motorola DynaTAC 1973. Cellular standards enabled mobile phone adoption.
cases.secondary: Massive global cellular network buildout (1980-2000s). AMPS standard 1983 enabled US rollout. GSM standard 1991 enabled global roaming. CDMA/3G standards 1990s-2000s. Millions of towers built globally. US spectrum auctions 1994 raised $7 billion, drove competition. Ongoing operator capex billions annually.
third_order: Smartphone ecosystem (iPhone 2007, Android)
Mobile applications and app market
Mobile location-based services (converged with GPS)
Text messaging and mobile communication dominance
cases.transmission_mechanism: Global cellular infrastructure was prerequisite for smartphones. Towers built primarily for voice; data networks (3G/4G late 2000s) specifically enabled smartphone viability. Transmission mechanism weaker than other cases: smartphones depended on ongoing network investment rather than repurposing stranded overcapacity from prior bubble.
cases.who_captured_value: Network operators (AT&T, Verizon, European carriers) captured subscription value. Apple and Google captured platform value. Motorola DynaTAC inventors lost competitive position.
cases.counterfactual: Without cellular infrastructure, smartphones could not operate. However, smartphones also depended on separate semiconductor improvements, separate GPS accuracy improvements, and software platforms. This makes third-order causation less isolatable than other cases.

cases.name: Containerization and Global Supply Chains
cases.primary: Containerization invented 1950s. ISO international standard established 1972 (20-ft and 40-ft containers standardized). Provided reliable, standardized shipping method.
cases.secondary: Massive port infrastructure transformation (1970s-1980s). Old general-cargo ports became obsolete. New container-focused port infrastructure built/retrofitted (container cranes, handling equipment). Container ships designed and manufactured. Old port worker skills became less relevant (disruption). Large capex in ports globally.
third_order: Global supply chains enabled
Just-in-time manufacturing
Manufacturing outsourcing to low-cost countries (Asia)
Integrated global production networks
Intermediate goods traded globally
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cost and reliability threshold crossed. Pre-container: general cargo ~$5/ton (1960s), unreliable (damage common), slow (manual loading). Post-container: predictable cost (~$0.50-1.00/ton by 1980s), fast, reliable, no damage. Cost reduction crossed geographic arbitrage threshold: developing-country labor savings exceeded shipping cost, enabling global production networks.
cases.who_captured_value: Shipping companies captured some value. Manufacturers (Nike, electronics) captured value via outsourcing. Walmart and retail platforms captured value via efficient sourcing. Port infrastructure investors captured some returns.
cases.counterfactual: Without containerization standardization enabling reliable global shipping, global supply chains and manufacturing outsourcing to Asia would have been delayed decades. Cost and complexity of distributing intermediate goods globally would have been prohibitive.

cases.name: Dot-com/Telecom Fibre Bubble and Cloud Computing
cases.primary: Internet commercialization and TCP/IP standardization (1991-1995). WWW released publicly 1991. Mosaic browser 1993. AOL IPO 1992 enabled consumer internet.
cases.secondary: Massive dot-com and telecom bubble (1995-2001). Telecommunications Act 1996 deregulated long-distance and enabled carrier competition. Venture capital flooded ISPs and web companies. Telecom carriers (MCI, WorldCom, Sprint, Qwest, Global Crossing, Level 3) engaged in massive fibre buildout racing to capture long-distance traffic. Estimated 2+ million miles fibre laid in US during 1990s-2000s. Major bankruptcies signaled overcapacity: WorldCom (2002, largest US bankruptcy to date), Global Crossing (2001). Much infrastructure became dark fibre (unused capacity).
third_order: Cloud computing (AWS 2006, Azure, Google Cloud)
CDNs (Akamai scaled 1998-2005)
Hyperscale data centers
Streaming video (YouTube 2005, Netflix 2007)
Entire digital platform economy
cases.transmission_mechanism: Multiple mechanisms: (1) Stranded asset repurposing: overcapacity fibre → dark fibre purchased cheaply by cloud providers; (2) Skills spillover: telecom engineers transferred to cloud companies understanding large-scale networks; (3) Price collapse enabling threshold: bandwidth cost fell $100/Mbps/month (1995) to $1/Mbps/month (2005), crossing streaming video viability threshold; (4) Standardization: telecom buildout created TCP/IP maturity, BGP routing standards, equipment interoperability.
cases.who_captured_value: Telecom carriers lost billions and bankrupted (MCI, WorldCom, Global Crossing). Equipment vendors (Cisco, Ciena) captured some value. Cloud providers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google) captured enormous value. Streaming platforms (Netflix, YouTube) captured value. CDNs became viable business.
cases.counterfactual: Without telecom overcapacity and resulting dark fibre availability, cloud computing economics would have been prohibitive (bandwidth costs too high). Streaming video would not have been viable business model. AWS, Netflix at scale, and hyperscale cloud would have faced fundamental cost constraints.

cases.name: Smartphone supply chain → component cost collapse → drones/EVs/IoT
cases.primary: Smartphone market explosion (iPhone 2007, Android 2009+); global shipments scale from 150M (2009) to 1.5B+ (2015)
cases.secondary: Massive capex in battery, MEMS sensor, camera, and RF chip manufacturing to serve smartphone demand; lithium-ion overcapacity; cost curves collapse from production volume
third_order: Drone category creation (DJI Phantom 2012+) using commodity smartphone sensors and batteries at sub-$100/kWh
Electric vehicle scaling (Tesla Model S/3) enabled by low-cost battery packs that were not economically viable pre-smartphone volume
IoT and wearable device ecosystems viable only at smartphone-scale component costs
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cost-curve collapse crossing economic threshold: lithium-ion cells fell from $600/kWh (2010) to $80-100/kWh (2020). Below ~$100/kWh, vehicle-scale battery packs became viable; above $300/kWh, they were economical only for niche applications. MEMS accelerometer, camera, and RF chip miniaturization spillover enabled drone payload sensor suites that were not possible at pre-smartphone costs.
cases.who_captured_value: DJI, Tesla, IoT platform companies (not original phone makers). Capex accrued to battery manufacturers and contract electronics suppliers.
cases.lag_years: 3-5 years secondary-to-third visible; 10-12 years primary-to-full-deployment
cases.counterfactual: Without smartphone volume scaling, battery and sensor cost curves would flatten at much higher price points. Lithium-ion would remain luxury-good pricing ($400-500/kWh); MEMS accelerometers stay at $5-10/unit. EVs and drones remain niche or nonexistent in this timeline.
cases.fourth_order: Renewable energy grid transformation enabled by EVs as distributed storage; autonomous vehicles becoming feasible due to low-cost MEMS and compute
sources: Tesla shareholder letters (battery cost evolution by model year)
DJI teardowns and public disclosures on sensor/battery sourcing
IVL Swedish Battery Report on supply chain

cases.name: GPU scaling for gaming → CUDA ecosystem maturation → deep learning revolution
cases.primary: NVIDIA CUDA release (2007); gaming GPU compute demand scaling (DirectX 11, OpenGL 4.0); gaming revenue $7B (2008) → $20B+ (2015)
cases.secondary: Overcapacity in parallel-compute silicon; CUDA software ecosystem maturation (documentation, libraries, deployment tooling); GPUs become general-purpose (GPGPU trend); GDDR memory abundant and cheap
third_order: Deep learning revolution (AlexNet 2012, first modern CNN trained on NVIDIA GPU)
TensorFlow, Caffe, PyTorch frameworks all optimized for CUDA GPUs
Google, Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft scaled foundation models on GPU clusters; ChatGPT, BERT, vision transformers all GPU-trained
cases.transmission_mechanism: Ecosystem lock-in + architectural fit: Deep learning requires massive parallel matrix multiplication—exactly what GPUs do. CUDA software ecosystem was already mature and documented from gaming demand, dramatically reducing friction for DL adoption. GPU memory architecture (fast GDDR, high bandwidth) matched DL training requirements better than CPU architectures. Without prior gaming demand, CUDA would not exist; without ecosystem maturity, early DL adoption would have been slower and more fragmented.
cases.who_captured_value: Google, Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft (not NVIDIA initially; NVIDIA captured value later as AI demand exploded post-2017)
cases.lag_years: 4-6 years from secondary peak to AlexNet/DL inflection point
cases.counterfactual: Pre-gaming-GPU, CUDA did not exist. TPUs and other accelerators emerged later (Google 2015+), but by then CUDA network effects and lock-in were strong. DL adoption would have been fragmented across multiple architectures rather than GPU-dominant.
cases.fourth_order: Emergence of AI-specific silicon (TPUs, Tracer, Habana, Graphcore) as competitive alternatives; GPU architecture arms race; NVIDIA market cap expansion from $15B (2012) to $3T+ (2024)
sources: TensorFlow, PyTorch documentation citing NVIDIA GPU architecture
NVIDIA CUDA adoption timeline and release notes (official)
Google Cloud TPU announcement and rationale (2015)

cases.name: US shale oil/gas overcapacity → cheap natural gas → Gulf Coast petrochemical renaissance
cases.primary: Hydraulic fracturing innovation enables shale extraction; horizontal drilling maturation; US natural gas production scales from ~1 Bcf/day (2008) to 5+ Bcf/day (2014)
cases.secondary: Massive glut of natural gas; prices collapse from $13/mmBtu (2008) to $2-3/mmBtu (2012-2014); overcapacity in production and export infrastructure (LNG terminals: Sabine Pass, Freeport, etc.)
third_order: Gulf Coast petrochemical capacity explosion (Exxon Beaumont, LyondellBasell expansions, Huntsman new plants, others)
US returned to net petrochemical exporter (post-1980s decline reversed)
US undercut Middle Eastern producers on polyethylene, propylene, and other basic chemicals; global trade flows realigned
cases.transmission_mechanism: Feedstock cost asymmetry enabling new capacity: petrochemical production is 60-70% feedstock cost (ethane, propane, methane). Price reduction from $13 to $3/mmBtu = >50% cost reduction in largest cost bucket. This crossed economic threshold where new Gulf Coast plants undercut existing Middle East capacity. Producers built capacity they could not have justified at prior gas prices (was a capital-destroying business above $8/mmBtu).
cases.who_captured_value: Petrochemical producers (Dow, LyondellBasell, Huntsman); not natural gas producers themselves (who earned commodity returns)
cases.lag_years: 4-7 years from shale primary to full third-order buildout visible (2008 shale primary → 2012-2018 capex announcements)
cases.counterfactual: At $13/mmBtu gas, Gulf Coast petrochemical plants were economically marginal vs. Middle East. Cost curve collapse to $3/mmBtu was necessary condition for new capacity buildout. Without shale, US petrochemical industry would have continued terminal decline.
cases.fourth_order: Global petrochemical price arbitrage and trade realignment; pressure on Asian crackers; European chemical industry structural stress (compounded by 2022 energy crisis)
sources: US EIA natural gas spot prices and production data
LyondellBasell, Dow investor relations docs citing cheap gas feedstock as capex driver

cases.name: Chinese solar manufacturing overcapacity → LCOE collapse → electricity-intensive industries
cases.primary: Chinese solar panel manufacturing scale-up; global production 40 GW (2010) → 227 GW (2015); race to volume; massive fabs capex
cases.secondary: Industry overcapacity; module prices collapse from $1.50/W (2010) to $0.50/W (2015) to $0.20-30/W (2020); LCOE drops from $300-400/MWh (2010) to $40-60/MWh (2020); sub-$30/MWh in sunbelt regions by 2020
third_order: Cryptocurrency mining moved to Iceland, El Salvador, N. Africa seeking <$30/MWh electricity (2018-2021)
AI datacentres seeking cheap renewable power (Google, Microsoft, Meta announcements 2022+)
Green hydrogen electrolyzers becoming cost-competitive vs. steam methane reforming (2020+)
Aluminum smelting renewed interest in cheap-power locations
cases.transmission_mechanism: Cost-curve collapse crossing new-industry threshold: below ~$30/MWh electricity, energy-intensive processes become economically viable where they were not at $300/MWh. At sub-$50/MWh, green hydrogen crosses parity with SMR. At sub-$30/MWh, crypto mining becomes profitable even at modest BTC prices; AI inference margins at datacentre scale become viable. Second-order overcapacity forced prices to these threshold points; third-order industries sprung up to consume cheap electricity.
cases.who_captured_value: Crypto miners, AI datacentre operators, hydrogen startups (not Chinese panel makers, who faced margin compression)
cases.lag_years: 5-8 years from secondary peak to third-order emergence
cases.counterfactual: At $300/MWh electricity (2010 baseline), none of these industries (crypto mining for scale, AI inference centers, green hydrogen) are economically viable. Cost collapse to sub-$30/MWh was threshold-crossing event enabling new categories.
cases.fourth_order: Unclear as of 2026; depends on materialization of hydrogen economy, AI inference decentralization, industrial process electrification
sources: IRENA Renewable Cost and Performance Database 2024
Bitcoin mining hash rate migration data (blockchain analysis, mining pools)
Google Workspace blog on renewable energy procurement (2022+)
Microsoft climate research on carbon-free datacentres

cases.name: COVID-19 mRNA vaccine success → platform investment → oncology/disease pipeline
cases.primary: COVID-19 pandemic; emergency authorization for mRNA vaccines (Moderna Dec 2020, BioNTech/Pfizer Dec 2020); proof-of-concept for mRNA platform at scale
cases.secondary: Massive public/private investment in mRNA manufacturing and clinical infrastructure; Moderna ~$2B capex, BioNTech ~$1.5B capex; FDA/EMA establish mRNA regulatory pathways; workforce (manufacturing, clinical, regulatory) scales up
third_order: Oncology development programs (Moderna BNT111 ovarian cancer Phase 2, others; BioNTech BNT211, BNT112 melanoma Phase 1/2)
Flu and RSV programs launched by Moderna, BioNTech (GSK partnership)
CureVac, other biotech pursuing mRNA platforms
mRNA accepted by regulators as validated platform modality
cases.transmission_mechanism: Platform validation + capital + expertise spillover: COVID vaccines proved mRNA could (a) manufacture at scale, (b) generate robust immune response, (c) reach market rapidly. Regulatory acceptance by FDA/EMA reduced downstream risk for new indications. Capital and manufacturing expertise from vaccine programs flowed into disease applications (oncology, infectious disease). Expertise in rapid clinical development transferred.
cases.who_captured_value: Biotech companies (Moderna, BioNTech); ultimate value capture unclear due to early-stage pipeline
cases.lag_years: 2-3 years from secondary peak to visible third-order programs
cases.counterfactual: Pre-COVID, mRNA oncology was highly speculative. Large-scale manufacturing did not exist; regulatory pathway was uncertain. COVID provided platform validation and capital that would have taken 5-10 years to accumulate through traditional biotech channels.
cases.fourth_order: Too early to judge (2026); depends on oncology program success rates and long clinical timelines (5-10 years to approval)
sources: BioNTech investor presentations and press releases
GSK partnership with Moderna on RSV/flu (press release 2022)

cases.name: Cryptocurrency mining infrastructure buildout → stranded capacity → redeployment to AI/datacentres
cases.primary: Bitcoin/crypto price spike and mining profitability surge (BTC $400 2015 → $13k late 2017; Ethereum rise); mining capex boom
cases.secondary: Overcapacity in GPU/ASIC manufacturing and datacentres (2017-2021); ~$5-10B estimated infrastructure capex; mining operations built in Iceland, El Salvador, Kazakhstan, China seeking cheap power; long-term power contracts signed for hydro, geothermal, wind
third_order: Bitcoin price crash (Nov 2021 peak $69k → Dec 2022 low $16k); mining profitability collapsed
Datacentre capacity repurposed for AI/ML training and inference (2022-2024)
GPU supply freed up from mining for AI compute (easing GPU shortage 2023-2024)
Renewable power contracts in Iceland, other low-cost regions repurposed for AI datacentres
cases.transmission_mechanism: Stranded-asset repurposing + infrastructure/skill transfer: Mining boom built high-density datacentres and secured power contracts in locations not previously attractive (Iceland geothermal, Kazakhstan hydro). When crypto crashed, that infrastructure did not evaporate. Turns out those locations are excellent for AI datacentres (want cheap electricity + natural cooling). Know-how in high-density compute cluster operations transferred. GPU supply chains built for mining became available for AI.
cases.who_captured_value: AI companies, cloud hyperscalers (Google, Microsoft, Meta), datacentre operators; not crypto miners themselves
cases.lag_years: 3-4 years from secondary peak to visible redeployment
cases.counterfactual: Without crypto mining boom, those datacentres and power contracts would not exist. When AI demand spiked (2023), hyperscalers benefited from stranded infrastructure they did not build. With different timing, that capacity might have been scrapped rather than repurposed.
cases.fourth_order: Unclear as of 2026; depends on whether AI compute concentrates in hyperscaler regions or distributes to renewable-power locations
sources: Bitcoin blockchain data (hash rate, difficulty, price history)
Iceland Ministry of Industries public records on datacentre permits
Google/Microsoft/Meta announcements on renewable energy for AI datacentres

cases.name: Electricity-to-Assembly-Line Narrative Conflation
cases.primary: Invention and commercialization of AC electric motors and grid electrification (Tesla, Westinghouse, Edison)
cases.secondary: Shift from centralized line-shaft factory power systems to distributed individual-motor setups; widespread factory electrification across US and Europe
third_order: Assembly-line mass production systems
Cheap mass-produced automobiles
Industrial capacity for WWII
cases.transmission_mechanism: CONTESTED: The operator's canonical claim is electricity → factory floor reorganization → assembly line. But evidence suggests factories began reorganizing to batch-produce identical goods BEFORE widespread electrification (reorganization occurred 1880s; US grid electrification accelerated 1905-1920). The shift from line-shaft to individual electric motors WAS enabled by electricity, but this may be coincident with assembly-line adoption, not causal to it. Both were driven by demand for mass-produced identical goods. David Nye (Electrifying America) argues electrification was result, not cause, of prior reorganization drives. The mechanistic causal claim lacks experimental evidence.
cases.who_captured_value: Automakers and appliance manufacturers captured the assembly-line efficiency surplus (Ford, GM). GE benefited from motor sales, but the durable competitive advantage went to mass manufacturers.
cases.counterfactual: Would assembly-line manufacturing have emerged without electric motors? Yes, likely with minor delay. The constraint was economic (demand for identical goods), not technical. Electric motors made certain layouts more efficient, but labor specialization and mechanical flow (core assembly-line innovation) were independent of electrification. Steam power could have powered assembly lines, albeit less flexibly.
cases.lag_years: 20-30 years from initial electrification to dominant assembly-line adoption
cases.fourth_order: Suburban sprawl and mass consumer culture enabled by cheap cars, though beyond scope
sources: David Nye, Electrifying America: Social Meanings of a New Technology (MIT Press, 1990)
Thomas Hughes, Networks of Power: Electrification in Western Society 1880-1930 (Johns Hopkins, 1983)

cases.name: Dot-Com Dark Fiber Narrative Is Mechanically Wrong
cases.primary: Packet-switching internet technology and commercial TCP/IP deployment
cases.secondary: Dot-com bubble: ~$2 trillion invested in fiber-optic capacity by telecom providers (Worldcom, Level3, Qwest, etc.); ~$1 trillion+ lost in crash (2000-2003)
third_order: AWS and cloud computing services
Netflix and streaming media
SaaS applications
cases.transmission_mechanism: CONTESTED—THE MECHANISM IS WRONG: The canonical claim is that the dot-com bubble laid 'dark fiber' that AWS exploited. But this confuses causality. AWS (launched 2006) did not use layer-2 bubble infrastructure; it used wholesale capacity from carriers (Cogent, Internap) founded AFTER the crash to buy stranded assets cheaply. This is not 'layer-2 enabled layer-3'; it's 'layer-2 collapse enabled new entrants to acquire assets at distressed prices.' Different mechanism entirely. The fiber was built regardless; what changed was who could afford to buy it and on what terms.
cases.who_captured_value: AWS and cloud vendors captured value. The original fiber builders (Worldcom et al.) mostly bankrupted. Value transfer went to new entrants (Amazon), not from layer-2 enablement.
cases.counterfactual: Would AWS have emerged without the dot-com crash? Almost certainly yes, 1-2 years later. Amazon had capital, retail infrastructure, and data-management incentives independent of the bubble. AWS would have paid market rates for fiber instead of wholesale distressed rates. The bubble accelerated growth, not fundamentally enabled it.
cases.lag_years: 6-7 years from crash (2000-2001) to AWS launch (2006)
cases.fourth_order: Containerization/orchestration (Docker, Kubernetes) as cloud-native paradigms, weakly connected to fiber narrative

cases.name: 3G Spectrum Bubble: Pure Malinvestment, No Third Order
cases.primary: 3G (UMTS) mobile technology standardization and spectrum allocation
cases.secondary: Auction-driven bubble: UK (2000) £22.5B, Germany €30.6B, France €30.6B for 3G rights; European telcos paid ~€130B total; many overextended and bankrupted
cases.transmission_mechanism: ABSENT. 3G capacity was built, but it enabled mobile networks, not a new category of business. Mobile internet existed conceptually before 3G; Netflix (2007) emerged independently requiring broadband fiber, not 3G. Mobile apps (post-2008) could have run on 2G with degraded but functional performance. The spectrum value was extracted by incumbent carriers as rent, not redistributed to enable new business classes. No forced reorganization of telecom business models occurred.
cases.who_captured_value: Incumbent mobile carriers (Vodafone, Telecom Italia, etc.) captured spectrum rights and extracted consumer value via higher data charges. This was wealth transfer from consumers, not productive capacity creation.
cases.counterfactual: Without the 3G bubble, would mobile data have emerged? Yes—via 4G/LTE (5-10 years later) or Wi-Fi subsidies. 3G was a commercial transition technology that failed to achieve promised ROI. Pure malinvestment.
cases.lag_years: Not applicable; no third order emerged by 2025
sources: William Melody, Telecom Reform: Principles, Policies and Regulatory Practice (Technical University of Denmark, 1997)
Business Week, The $100 Billion Wireless Flop (August 2002)

cases.name: Subprime Housing Bubble: Destructive, Not Reorganizational
cases.primary: Mortgage origination technology and securitization (MBS, CDOs)
cases.secondary: Housing overbuilding: US starts peaked 2.27M (2006); excess inventory ~2M units. Subprime originations rose 8% (2003) to 20% (2006). Total loss ~$2-3 trillion home equity.
cases.transmission_mechanism: ABSENT/DESTRUCTIVE. The bubble destroyed housing production and finance, not reorganized it. Post-2009, housing starts collapsed to 0.55M (2009). Claimed third order: fintech and robo-advisory. But Zillow and Redfin existed BEFORE the crash (Zillow founded 2006), and fintech (Robinhood, Wealthfront) emerged 2010+ from Moore's Law and mobile technology, not housing crisis. The transmission mechanism ('crisis forced financial innovation') is post-hoc narrative, not evidence.
cases.who_captured_value: Financial engineers captured value during bubble; post-crash, value destroyed and transferred to taxpayers via TARP. No new business class enabled.
cases.counterfactual: Would fintech have emerged without the subprime crash? Almost certainly yes. Fintech was driven by semiconductor cost curves and regulatory arbitrage, not housing collapse. Destructive malinvestment with negative third-order effects.
cases.lag_years: No productive lag; value destroyed, not redirected
sources: Charles Morris, The Trillion Dollar Meltdown (PublicAffairs, 2008)
Bethany McLean and Joe Nocera, All the Devils Are Here (Portfolio, 2010)

cases.name: Blockchain/ICO Bubble: Infrastructure Exists But Utility Remains Unclear
cases.primary: Bitcoin invention (2009) and smart-contract platforms (Ethereum 2015)
cases.secondary: ICO bubble (2017-2018): ~$6.3B raised; most projects failed/fraudulent. Secondary bubble (2021): >$14 trillion crypto market cap at peak.
third_order: Stablecoins and DeFi protocols (though with contested productivity)
cases.transmission_mechanism: UNCLEAR/CONTESTED. Blockchain infrastructure exists, but enabled low-utility services. Stablecoins (USDC, USDT) primarily enable speculation and capital flight, not productive commerce. DeFi (Aave, Compound) replicates traditional finance on-chain with worse user economics (gas fees, complexity) for most users. Unlike fiber (reusable for any data application), most ICO code was abandoned and enabled speculation only. Ethereum transaction volume ($billions/day) is <0.1% of traditional finance. No new business category dependent on blockchain has achieved scale.
cases.who_captured_value: Early speculators and successful project founders (Vitalik Buterin, Ethereum core team) captured wealth via token appreciation. This is value extraction from later entrants, not value creation. Productive value captured is minimal.
cases.counterfactual: Without the ICO bubble, would blockchain have developed? Almost certainly yes. Bitcoin and Ethereum were created pre-bubble, driven by cryptographic innovation. The bubble may have accelerated research but did not enable it. This is technological foundation + speculative bubble with minimal third-order economic value.
cases.lag_years: 5+ years; insufficient time to assess. Major productive applications have not emerged by 2025.
sources: Molly White, The Bullish Case for Bitcoin Is Weaker Than You Think (2022)
Paul Krugman, The Mechanisms of Mania (New York Times, 2022)

cases.name: Productivity Paradox: Third Order Only Visible Retrospectively
cases.primary: Microprocessor and computer technology (Intel 4004 1971+); widespread enterprise IT adoption
cases.secondary: Office reorganization around computers; widespread adoption in clerical/admin roles; creation of IT departments and skill sets
third_order: E-commerce, digital information services, software-as-a-service (emerged 1990s+)
cases.transmission_mechanism: DELAYED AND UNPREDICTABLE, exposing hindsight bias. Erik Brynjolfsson's 1993 study found weak productivity correlation with computer investment through 1980s—the core puzzle of the 'productivity paradox.' If layer-2 reorganization was happening (computers in offices), where was layer-3 value? Claimed answer: e-commerce and digital services (1990s+). But this was NOT predictable from primary innovation. Observers in 1975 and 1985 could not foresee that computers would enable online retail. The transmission mechanism became visible only retrospectively.
cases.who_captured_value: Software companies (Microsoft, Oracle, SAP) captured value, not hardware makers or clerical workers. Aggregate productivity gains (0.5-1.5% annual acceleration 1995-2005) were broad-based, not captured by specific layer-3 business class.
cases.counterfactual: If observers in 1980 possessed this theory, could they have predicted e-commerce and digital services by 1995? Almost certainly no. The theory works only retrospectively, creating illusion of predictive power. Historical narrative is constructed post-hoc.
cases.lag_years: 20-30 years from primary innovation (1970s) to clear third-order business emergence (1990s-2000s)
cases.fourth_order: Cloud computing (2006+), AI/ML services (2010s+) appear as separate waves, not direct descendants of computer adoption
sources: Erik Brynjolfsson, The Productivity Paradox of Information Technology (Communications of the ACM, 1993)
Paul David, Computer and Dynamo: The Modern Productivity Paradox (OECD, 1990)

cases.name: Railway Overcapacity: Necessary But Not Causal to Assembly Line
cases.primary: Railway expansion and infrastructure standardization (gauge, coupling, switching)
cases.secondary: US rail overbuilding (1880s-1910s); many lines unprofitable; industry consolidation and bankruptcies
third_order: Assembly-line mass production
cases.transmission_mechanism: CONTESTED. The claim is that rail overcapacity provided logistics infrastructure enabling assembly-line distribution. But the transmission is logistics provision, not organizational reorganization. Rail did NOT teach manufacturers how to organize assembly lines; that was organizational innovation driven by market demand for identical goods. Rail was NECESSARY (for coal, steel input; finished goods output) but not SUFFICIENT to cause assembly-line adoption. Causality runs bidirectionally: assembly-line manufacturing created demand for cheap rail transport. This is complementary infrastructure, not causal chain.
cases.who_captured_value: Consolidated rail trusts (Union Pacific, ATSF) captured consolidation value. Assembly-line surplus went to automakers (Ford, GM). Rail overbuilding did not transfer value.
cases.counterfactual: Would assembly-line manufacturing have emerged without rail overcapacity? Yes, probably with minor delay. Motor trucks and improved roads (1910s+) provided alternative distribution. The core innovation (specialized labor + mechanical flow) was independent of rail. Rail was enabling infrastructure, not primary cause.
cases.lag_years: 20-30 years from peak rail building (1880s-1890s) to assembly-line dominance (1910s-1920s)
cases.fourth_order: Suburban sprawl enabled by reliable rail and auto transport

cases.name: Nuclear Power: Capital-Intensive Bubble, No Third Order
cases.primary: Nuclear fission technology for electricity generation (Atoms for Peace initiative)
cases.secondary: Massive overinvestment in nuclear plants; overoptimistic forecasts ('too cheap to meter'); regulatory capture; construction cost overruns 2-4x initial estimates
cases.transmission_mechanism: ABSENT. No third-order business category was enabled by nuclear power. Nuclear provided baseload electricity but did not reorganize power generation or enable new industries dependent on it. Expected third order (ubiquitous cheap electricity enabling new industries) failed because: (a) costs rose, not fell; (b) regulatory burden increased; (c) alternative sources (natural gas) proved cheaper and more flexible. Nuclear is paradigmatic capital-intensive malinvestment producing stranded assets (Vogtle, Diablo Canyon, UK AGRs), not productive capacity.
cases.who_captured_value: Utilities captured rate-regulated monopoly value; taxpayers subsidized cost overruns. Technology vendors (Westinghouse, GE) captured early value, then faced declining markets.
cases.counterfactual: Without nuclear investment, electricity would have been sourced from coal, hydro, or gas with similar aggregate output. No industry reorganization expected from nuclear power occurred.
cases.lag_years: 50+ years; no productive third order emerged by 2025

cases.name: Hindsight Bias: Third-Derivative Theory Works Only Retrospectively
cases.primary: The third-derivative framework as explanatory narrative device
cases.secondary: Adoption of the framework in business and economic literature (Carlota Perez, business strategists) as explanatory model
third_order: Investment decisions and policy based on prospective application of the framework
cases.transmission_mechanism: CRITICAL FLAW: The framework works perfectly retrospectively (electricity → factory reorganization → assembly line is coherent, plausible post-hoc narrative) but has NEVER successfully predicted a third order before it emerged. Historical records show: (a) observers in 1890, 1970, 2000 did NOT foresee the third order; (b) all detailed narratives were constructed AFTER emergence; (c) alternative narratives fit the same data (assembly lines could be explained by market demand independent of electricity; e-commerce could be explained by consumer preference independent of computers). If the theory only works retrospectively, it is descriptive, not predictive. Investors and policymakers using it prospectively are engaging in survivorship bias—seeing winners (electricity, internet) while ignoring losers (nuclear, 3G, space exploration).
cases.who_captured_value: Consultants, academics, and narrative-builders (Perez, business strategists) captured prestige and book sales. Investors using the framework prospectively lost capital on failed bets (nuclear, 3G, cleantech).
cases.counterfactual: If the framework has genuine predictive power, documented forecasts should exist from before third-order emergence (e.g., predictions in 1995 that internet would enable cloud computing by 2010). None are evident in academic or business literature. The theory is post-hoc rationalization.
cases.lag_years: N/A
cases.fourth_order: N/A
sources: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (Edward Elgar, 2002)
Nassim Taleb, Fooled by Randomness (Random House, 2001)

cases.name: US Airline Deregulation
cases.primary: Airline Deregulation Act eliminates Civil Aeronautics Board route monopolies and price controls
cases.secondary: New carrier entry (People Express, Midway, New York Air); fleet overbuild; hub infrastructure duplication; industry returns collapse to negative (1983-1985); hundreds of bankruptcies, route abandonments, stranded aircraft and pilot labor
third_order: Southwest Airlines point-to-point model
Budget carriers capturing 25% of US market by 2000
Leisure travel boom; passenger volume doubles
High-frequency automated scheduling becomes industry standard
cases.transmission_mechanism: Deregulation forced capacity competition. Overbuild and bankruptcies created (1) abandoned profitable regional routes available for new entry, (2) cheap aircraft leases and excess pilot labor supply, (3) proof that high-frequency automated scheduling beats legacy hub-and-spoke. Southwest's model was legally impossible under CAB; it required layer-2's capacity crisis and asset glut.
cases.who_captured_value: Budget carriers (Southwest, Spirit, Frontier, Allegiant) and consumers (lower fares). NOT legacy carriers (American, TWA, Eastern) who invested in overcapacity.
cases.counterfactual: Without deregulation-driven overcapacity, cheap aircraft and proven low-cost model would not exist. Southwest thrived because predecessors failed. Under CAB, Southwest's model would have been denied permission.
sources: Kellogg, R. (2011) Learning by Doing in Markets. AER.
Morrison, S. and Winston, C. (1995) The Evolution of the Airline Industry. Brookings

cases.name: ERISA and Institutional Asset Management
cases.primary: Employee Retirement Income Security Act mandates pension funding, fiduciary duty, professional management, and diversification
cases.secondary: Pension assets explode from $150B to $4T+ (1974-1990). Thousands of investment firms enter market. Performance benchmarking industry emerges. Overcapacity: intense fee competition, margin compression, many firms exit. Active management becomes commoditized.
third_order: Index funds become dominant (Vanguard 1976; 40%+ of institutional assets by 2000s)
Passive investing infrastructure and ETF industry
Modern portfolio theory becomes institutional standard
Shift to algorithmic and passive trading dominates
cases.transmission_mechanism: ERISA's fiduciary requirement created mandatory demand for institutional asset management. Asset explosion attracted thousands of entrants, causing overcapacity and fee wars. This commoditization made active management uneconomical, creating market for low-cost index funds. Index funds required prior layer-2 infrastructure: standardized performance measurement, centralized trading, settlement systems, trained talent pool.
cases.who_captured_value: Index fund providers (Vanguard, Fidelity, iShares, BlackRock). NOT the active managers who built overcapacity.
cases.fourth_order: Passive investing shifted from <1% (1975) to 40%+ (2010s), fundamentally reshaping capital allocation globally
cases.counterfactual: Index funds existed as concept before ERISA, but Vanguard's 1976 launch was only viable because ERISA created massive infrastructure demand, training, and benchmarking. Without layer-2 overcapacity, index funds would not have been economically viable.
sources: Merton, R.C. (1987) Capital Market Equilibrium with Incomplete Information. JF.

cases.name: The Black Death
cases.primary: Plague kills 30-60% of European population; recurs for 300+ years
cases.secondary: Massive labor shortage and wage crisis (1350-1380). Real wages for laborers double or triple. Serfdom becomes economically unsustainable. Peasant revolts (Peasants' Revolt 1381, Jacquerie 1358). Wage-ceiling legislation (Ordinance of Labourers 1349) fails due to labor mobility. Feudal system breakdown.
third_order: End of serfdom across Western Europe (effective by 1500)
Rise of free wage-labor farming and tenant farming
Agricultural investment shift from labor extraction to tools, mills, drainage
Urbanization (rural exodus)
Foundation for wage-labor capitalism and competitive labor markets
cases.transmission_mechanism: Labor scarcity inverted power structure. Lords attempted wage ceilings and serfdom enforcement but failed—labor mobility and scarcity gave workers bargaining power. Layer-2 reorganization: forced transition from forced labor to wage labor. Once wage labor became standard, institutional framework shifted: labor became commodity in markets, creating incentives for capital investment in productivity rather than coercion. Free labor markets became foundation for capitalist production.
cases.who_captured_value: Surviving peasants and wage laborers (higher real wages for 200+ years). Long-term: landowners adapting to capitalist agriculture. NOT feudal lords who lost direct labor control.
cases.fourth_order: Industrial capitalism and Industrial Revolution (18th-19th century) would have been impossible in feudal labor system. Demographic shock forced institutional transformation enabling capitalism.
cases.counterfactual: European feudalism could have persisted centuries longer without Black Death forcing labor scarcity. Lords attempted legislative enforcement (Ordinance) but failed because supply shock removed leverage. Wage crisis forced reorganization; only then capitalism possible.
sources: Brenner, R. (1976) Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development. P&P.
Clark, G. (2007) A Farewell to Alms. Princeton UP.

cases.name: Bayh-Dole Act
cases.primary: Bayh-Dole Act allows universities and small firms to own patents on federally-funded research (overturning prior government ownership)
cases.secondary: University tech-transfer office proliferation (1980-1995). Patent filings surge from <100/year (1970s) to >1000/year by 1990. Spin-off startups created. Overcapacity: nearly every university builds tech-transfer office; most operate at losses. Massive hiring of licensing professionals and lawyers.
third_order: Biotech industry clustering in Boston, San Francisco, San Diego
University-industry partnerships become standard
Venture capital flows to areas near research universities
Modern pharmaceutical R&D model based on university-pharma linkages
cases.transmission_mechanism: Bayh-Dole created IP incentives for universities, triggering infrastructure investment. Overcapacity phase (most tech-transfer offices at losses) necessary to: build legal/administrative licensing infrastructure, standardize licensing agreements, create startup mentorship models, build geographic clusters enabling knowledge spillover. Biotech clusters required this layer-2 infrastructure layering. However, concurrent molecular biology breakthroughs (PCR, sequencing) also drove biotech, making causality contested.
cases.who_captured_value: Venture capital, biotech founders (Genentech, Biogen), eventually universities (as tech-transfer became profitable). NOT individual inventors/patent holders (minimal royalty shares).
cases.counterfactual: Biotech would have developed without Bayh-Dole (concurrent science breakthroughs drove it), but university-linked clusters would have been much smaller/slower. Layer-2 infrastructure and relationships built by tech-transfer offices crucial for accelerating cluster formation.
sources: Mowery, D.C., Nelson, R.R., Sampat, B.N., Ziedonis, A.A. (2015) Ivory Tower and Industrial Innovation. Stanford.
Sampat, B. (2006) Patenting and US Academic Research. RP.

cases.name: AT&T Breakup
cases.primary: Antitrust divestiture of Bell System; forced breakup into AT&T Long Lines and 7 Regional Bell Operating Companies (RBOCs)
cases.secondary: Infrastructure overbuild (1984-1995). RBOCs build duplicate local fiber networks. AT&T, MCI, Sprint compete for long-distance. Bell Labs split; equipment makers (Lucent, Nortel) spun out. Cost per call minute falls 90% via competition and redundancy. Massive overcapacity in switching/transmission. Many projects abandoned as technology moves past copper to fiber.
third_order: Internet Service Providers proliferate (1995-2000) using cheap RBOC infrastructure
Telecom equipment industry thrives (Cisco, Lucent, Nortel)
Software companies (Netscape, Yahoo) enable online services via cheap abundant connectivity
Broadband and e-commerce enabled by cost-collapsed telecom
cases.transmission_mechanism: Antitrust forced infrastructure competition. Redundant buildout created overcapacity and cost collapse (price per call minute fell 90% in 1990s). Open-access requirements forced RBOCs to lease capacity at regulated rates. This created commodity cheapness and open infrastructure ISPs needed. ISPs could not have thrived under Bell monopoly (which extracted rents and controlled services). Layer-2's overcapacity and forced open-access were prerequisites for layer-3.
cases.who_captured_value: ISPs (Earthlink, AOL, Prodigy), equipment makers (Cisco), software/internet companies (Netscape, Amazon), consumers (lower costs). NOT legacy Bell companies which lost monopoly rents.
cases.fourth_order: Internet dominance (1995-2020) built on cheap telecom that would not exist under Bell monopoly pricing
cases.counterfactual: Under Bell monopoly, ISPs faced monopoly pricing and network control. Breakup-driven overcapacity forced cost collapse and open access—prerequisites for internet scaling.
sources: Temin, P. (1987) The Fall of the Bell System. Cambridge.
Hazlett, T.W., Havenner, A. (2003) High-Tech Warfare: Lessons from AT&T Breakup. EIN.

cases.name: Post-WWII Japan: Zaibatsu Dissolution and Export-Driven Growth
cases.primary: US occupation forces zaibatsu (Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo, Yasuda) dissolution and economic restructuring
cases.secondary: Rapid manufacturing capacity rebuild (1950-1965). Factories rebuilt with latest (often US second-hand) machinery.
