Southwest Airlines was founded in 1971 and operated profitably as a Texas intrastate carrier for seven years precisely BECAUSE intrastate carriers were exempt from Civil Aeronautics Board regulation. The claim that 'Southwest's model was legally impossible under CAB' is false and inverts the case's mechanism: deregulation allowed geographic scaling of an already-proven model; the layer-2 asset glut did not create the model. (Verified this session.)

The skeptic case 'Dot-Com Dark Fiber Narrative Is Mechanically Wrong' is itself factually wrong: Cogent was founded in 1999 and Internap in 1996, both BEFORE the crash, not after. However, Cogent's record of acquiring roughly $14bn of book-value assets for about $60m in 2001-2004 is the single strongest verified evidence FOR the distressed-transfer mechanism. The skeptic case should be corrected in a direction that strengthens, not weakens, the operator. (Verified this session.)

Railway Mania -> British time standardization is chronologically inverted. Great Western Railway adopted London time in November 1840 and the Railway Clearing House recommended GMT in 1847; the 1844-47 Mania cannot have caused a standardization that began before it. The US 1883 time-zone adoption is correctly dated and belongs only under the US railroad case.

mRNA case contains three attribution errors: BNT111 is BioNTech's (not Moderna's) FixVac candidate in MELANOMA, not ovarian cancer; BNT112 is a prostate cancer candidate, not melanoma; Moderna's lead oncology asset is mRNA-4157/V940 (intismeran autogene) with Merck. The 'BNT' prefix denotes BioNTech, so 'Moderna BNT111' is self-evidently wrong.

Chinese solar -> crypto migration is not supported. Iceland has essentially no solar resource; its cheap power is geothermal and hydro. Kazakhstan mining ran on coal and Sichuan on hydro. PV LCOE did not drive that migration.

Solar figures conflate annual production with cumulative installed capacity: global annual PV module production in 2015 was roughly 60-70 GW; the ~227 GW figure is approximately the cumulative global installed base, not annual output.

Battery costs mix pack and cell prices. BNEF pack prices were roughly $1,100-1,200/kWh in 2010 and about $137/kWh in 2020 (cell about $100). '$600/kWh (2010) to $80-100/kWh (2020)' is not a like-for-like series.

The smartphone -> EV battery lineage names the wrong parent industry. Tesla's Roadster and Model S used 18650 cylindrical cells from the laptop and power-tool supply chain; smartphones use pouch cells and are a modest share of total lithium-ion cell volume. The correct claim is consumer-electronics-and-power-tool volume, not smartphone volume.

GPU case revenue figures are wrong: NVIDIA's TOTAL company revenue in FY2015 was about $4.7bn, with gaming around $2.8bn. '$7B (2008) to $20B+ (2015)' is not NVIDIA gaming revenue and is unsourced. CUDA was announced November 2006 with the SDK released in 2007.

Crypto -> AI is overstated. The 2023-24 shortage was in datacentre-class accelerators (A100/H100) with NVLink and liquid cooling, not consumer GPUs freed by Ethereum's September 2022 Merge; Bitcoin ASICs are useless for AI. The genuine and narrow instance is site, power-contract and shell reuse (CoreWeave, Core Scientific, Applied Digital), not silicon reuse.

Fluyt -> VOC mechanism is wrong. Fluyts were unarmed bulk carriers built for the Baltic grain, salt and timber trades and were largely not used on the Asia route, which required armed retourschepen. The VOC (1602) also predates the fluyt's mass diffusion. The defensible chain is Baltic 'mother trade' -> Amsterdam capital accumulation -> VOC, not 'fluyt enabled the Asian monopoly'.

Zaibatsu dissolution was substantially reversed. Of roughly 325 firms designated under the 1947 deconcentration law, only about nine to eleven were actually split before the 1948 'reverse course' halted the programme, and the groups reformed as bank-centred keiretsu in the 1950s. The case's layer-2 premise ('zaibatsu to lean competing firms') describes a reform that was mostly rescinded.

Eurodollar Cold War origin is a contested myth. Catherine Schenk's research locates the market's emergence in Midland Bank's 1955 dollar deposit arbitrage and the 1957 sterling crisis and UK exchange controls, not Soviet deposit flight. Keep the market, drop the Soviet causal framing.

Bayh-Dole patent counts are too low and the effect is overstated. US university patenting was in the low hundreds per year by the late 1970s and was already rising under pre-1980 Institutional Patent Agreements; Mowery, Nelson, Sampat and Ziedonis show growth concentrated in institutions already patenting before the Act.

Containerization's $5.83/ton to $0.16/ton pair derives from a single McLean Industries internal estimate for one 1956 sailing, reported in Levinson's 'The Box', where Levinson explicitly cautions against generalising it. It is presented here as an industry fact in two separate entries.

India 1991 mechanism is invented. TCS (1968), Infosys (1981) and Wipro's IT arm predate liberalization; the actual enabling factors were the 1986 software policy, STPI (1991), Y2K demand, US H-1B access and an expanding engineering-college pipeline. There is no documented flow of engineers laid off from collapsing protected sectors into IT services.

Apollo IC figures: the well-sourced claim is that Apollo consumed roughly 60% of US (not world) IC production in 1963, and bought on the order of one million ICs across the programme. '200,000+ circuits for AGC Block I testing' is not a standard figure, and Minuteman II was the larger single IC buyer by 1964-65.

Printing press mechanism rests on a contested thesis. Eisenstein's 'typographical fixity' is directly challenged by Adrian Johns ('The Nature of the Book', 1998), who argues fixity was a socially constructed achievement rather than a property of print, and that early printed texts were notoriously corrupt and pirated. Grading this 'strong' is not defensible.

Interstate Highway 'returns of $6-$1.80 per $1' splices two different periods from the Nadiri and Mamuneas / FHWA work: the high figure applies to the 1950s-60s build-out and returns fall toward or below $1 by the 1980s-90s. Presented as a range it implies uniformly high returns.

Telegraph case: 'half of London's telegraph traffic by the 1850s was stock-market data' has no source and could not be verified. The '75+ companies by 1851' figure conflates US and British counts; Britain had a near-duopoly (Electric Telegraph Company and British and Irish Magnetic).

ERISA case: 'index funds 40%+ of institutional assets by 2000s' is not supportable at that date; passive crossed roughly half of US equity fund assets only around 2019. Airline case: low-cost carriers reached about 25% of US domestic capacity around 2005, not 2000.
strongest_named_concepts: General Purpose Technology theory with co-invention lag (Bresnahan & Trajtenberg 1995; Helpman 1998) - the formal economics name for layer 1 requiring complementary innovation before value appears

Complementary organisational capital / the dynamo-and-computer argument (Paul David 1990; Warren Devine 1983; Brynjolfsson & Hitt) - literally the source of the operator's own electricity example; names layer 2 as reorganisation and supplies the 40-year lag

Installation period / frenzy -> turning point -> deployment period / golden age (Carlota Perez, 'Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital', 2002) - names layer 2 as bubble, and her 2009 distinction between technology bubbles and easy-money asset-inflation bubbles is precisely the discriminator the operator is missing

The productive bubble / Schumpeterian waste (William Janeway, 'Doing Capitalism in the Innovative Economy', 2012) - the specific claim that only bubbles financing a durable capital object leave a usable residue
The productivity J-curve (Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson 2021) and the Solow productivity paradox - names the measured trough between layer 2 and layer 3
Unbalanced growth, forward linkages and social overhead capital (Hirschman 1958) - infrastructure built ahead of demand as a deliberate forcing function
Technological convergence, complementarities and 'focusing devices' (Nathan Rosenberg) - how a bottleneck in one sector directs innovation in another
Path dependence and lock-in (David; Brian Arthur) - why the overbuilt substrate constrains which layer 3 is reachable
The adjacent possible (Kauffman; Steven Johnson) - the unpredictability property, which is weaker than the operator assumes

COUNTER-LITERATURE the operator must engage: Goldfarb & Kirsch, 'Bubbles and Crashes: The Boom and Bust of Technological Innovation' (2019), which argues systematically that narrative and uncertainty, not infrastructure residue, are the recurring feature of technology bubbles, and that most leave little behind
cases_to_promote: AT&T divestiture (1982-84) -> forced open access -> ISPs. The cleanest case in the set because the enabling condition is a legal act with an observable counterfactual: telecom markets that did not force separation had markedly slower ISP formation. It also correctly isolates that the operative variable is forced separation, not overbuild.

Dot-com/telecom fibre -> cloud, CDN, streaming - but ONLY rebuilt around the verified distressed-transfer evidence (Cogent acquiring roughly $14bn book value for about $60m) plus the $/Mbps threshold, and with the vague 'AWS ran on dark fibre' claim deleted. The mechanism is title transfer at a 200:1 discount, which is specific, dated and checkable.

Apollo and Minuteman IC procurement -> learning-curve cost collapse -> minicomputers and PCs (with figures corrected to ~60% of US production in 1963). Best documented example of guaranteed government offtake buying down a manufacturing learning curve, and the layer-3 applications were known and priced out in advance.

US railroad overbuilding (1870s-90s) -> mail order and Chicago commodity markets. Documented in Cronon's 'Nature's Metropolis' and Chandler; the specific mechanism - overcapacity forcing marginal-cost freight pricing that Sears could exploit - is the operator's thesis in its most literal and best-evidenced form.

GPU/CUDA -> deep learning (with revenue figures corrected). The strongest MODERN case, and the most instructive: neural networks were described in the 1980s and explicitly known to be compute-blocked. It demonstrates that the third order was known in kind and unknown only in timing - which is the operator's most usable prospective handle.

The Black Death - promote specifically as the set's best natural experiment, and for the OPPOSITE reason the case file gives. Identical layer-1 shock and identical layer-2 labour scarcity produced the end of serfdom in Western Europe and the SECOND SERFDOM in Eastern Europe (the Brenner debate). Same shock, opposite third orders. This single case shows that institutions and bargaining power, not the shock or the overbuild, select layer 3 - and it should anchor the report's honest section.

Factory electrification (1900-1930) - promote in David's and Devine's corrected form only: unit drive freed plant layout from line-shaft geometry, with a roughly 40-year productivity lag. Explicitly NOT as 'electricity caused the assembly line', which the operator's own contested case correctly rejects.

US airline deregulation - promote with the Southwest correction, reframed: layer 2 supplied scale and cheap aircraft to a model already proven intrastate since 1971. This is a better case than the file makes it, because the corrected version separates 'invention of the model' from 'availability of distressed capacity', which is exactly the distinction the framework needs.
cases_to_drop: Bessemer Steel - has no second order at all. It is a pure input-cost curve with more downstream uses, which is just declining prices. Its inclusion shows the framework absorbing any cost-decline story, which is the strongest evidence for the unfalsifiability charge.

Printing press -> Scientific Revolution - the entire mechanism rests on Eisenstein's typographical-fixity thesis, directly contested by Adrian Johns; the layer-2 'overcapacity relative to demand' is asserted with zero evidence; and a 350-year lag makes the case unfalsifiable in principle.
Dutch fluyt -> VOC - mechanism is wrong (fluyts were not used on the armed Asia route) and the chronology is strained (VOC 1602 predates mass fluyt diffusion).
Mechanical refrigeration / cold chain - no supporting evidence, generic mechanism, and the layer-3 items (industrial monoculture) are normative judgements rather than value-capture claims.

Green Revolution - layer 2 is complementary input DEMAND, not overbuild; the mechanism runs backwards from the framework's own definition. Layer-3 items are contested normative claims about industrial agriculture.

Chinese solar -> crypto/AI/hydrogen - the crypto link is factually false (Iceland, Kazakhstan and Sichuan power is geothermal, coal and hydro, not solar), and the AI and hydrogen links are prospective assertions, not evidence.

COVID mRNA -> oncology pipeline - three factual mislabels, and more fundamentally it is a live PREDICTION being used as evidence for a framework whose disputed property is precisely its predictive validity. Circular.

Mobile cellular buildout - the case concedes its own mechanism is weak (ongoing operator capex, not stranded overcapacity from a bust). Either drop it or reclassify it as a negative case, which is what it actually is.

Containerization - the DUPLICATE entry must go. Two entries with different eras, mechanisms and evidence grades for the same event is itself a defect in the coding scheme and will be the first thing a hostile reader notices.

Securitization -> derivatives complex - drop or merge with the subprime case. As written the two entries contradict each other, and grading a $2-3trn value destruction as a successful third order demonstrates that the framework has no value sign.
Railway Mania -> British time standardization - chronologically inverted (Railway Time from 1840, before the Mania). Retain only the 1883 US time-zone adoption under the US railroad case.
Crypto -> AI datacentres - retain only the narrow, verifiable claim (site, power-contract and shell reuse: CoreWeave, Core Scientific). Delete the GPU-supply and ASIC claims entirely.
Eurodollar market - drop the Soviet Cold War origin narrative (contested by Schenk) and downgrade the remainder to weak; the layer-2 'overcapacity of offshore centres' is asserted, not shown.
Bayh-Dole - the case concedes confounding with PCR and sequencing, and the econometric literature finds a smaller effect than the narrative. Demote to illustrative, not evidential.

Interstate Highway System - the 'stranded rail assets freed capital' mechanism is asserted, and rail's decline was substantially a CONSEQUENCE of the highway subsidy. Layer 2 and layer 3 here are the same policy, so the case cannot support a causal chain.

'Hindsight Bias' meta-case - do not drop, but do not present it as one case among 41. It is the report's central finding and should be structural, not a row in a table. Presenting the critique as a case is itself a way of neutralising it.

completeness_critique:
## COMPLETENESS AUDIT — what twelve researchers and three verifiers never went looking for

---

## A. DISCIPLINES THAT WERE NEVER SEARCHED AT ALL

**A1. Transaction-cost economics / asset specificity.** Oliver Williamson — a Nobel laureate whose central concept, *asset specificity*, is precisely the variable that determines whether layer-2 wreckage can become layer-3 input — appears nowhere in 74 entries. Nor does the finance operationalisation of it (*asset redeployability*, Kim & Kung 2017), nor the macro version (*putty-clay vs putty-putty vintage capital*, Johansen/Solow).
→ *Question: Rank the 45 cases by an asset-redeployability measure (Williamson specificity, or Kim-Kung industry redeployability scores). Does redeployability, rather than "bubble-ness", separate the successes from nuclear/3G/subprime?*

**A2. The empirical economics of capital reallocation — the single largest hole.** The entire framework rests on stranded assets moving cheaply to new owners. There is a mature empirical literature on exactly this and none of it was cited: Shleifer & Vishny (1992) *Liquidation Values and Debt Capacity*; Pulvino (1998) on aircraft fire sales (which is literally the airline case); Ramey & Shapiro (2001, JPE) *Displaced Capital*, which measured aerospace plant liquidations and found equipment sold at roughly a quarter of replacement cost **with large real losses**; Eisfeldt & Rampini (2006), whose central finding is that **capital reallocation is procyclical — it is lowest in busts**, which cuts directly against the operator's mechanism.
→ *Question: Does Eisfeldt-Rampini procyclical reallocation falsify the claim that busts are when capacity changes hands productively? And what does Ramey-Shapiro's measured redeployment loss imply for how much of the fibre/rail/datacentre "residue" actually survived transfer?*

**A3. Bankruptcy and insolvency law as the enabling institution.** The verified Cogent datum ($14bn book for ~$60m) is a *Chapter 11 outcome*, not an economic law. Nobody asked whether the pattern is a US-legal-regime artefact. The obvious control is Japan post-1990: enormous infrastructure overbuild, banks forbore, assets never transferred, no third order. The zombie-lending literature (Caballero, Hoshi & Kashyap 2008; Banerjee & Hofmann at BIS) is absent.
→ *Question: Is "the third derivative" actually a function of liquidating bankruptcy regimes? Compare US telecom 2001-04 (assets transferred, layer 3 emerged) with Japanese real estate/construction 1991-2005 and European telecom post-3G (assets retained by incumbents, no layer 3).*

**A4. Economic geography and labour mobility.** No one asked *where* layer 3 appears. AnnaLee Saxenian's *Regional Advantage* (1994) — the definitive study of whether skills residue is portable, and why Route 128's collapse produced nothing while Silicon Valley's produced everything — is absent, as are Marshallian agglomeration, Jacobs externalities, and the inventor-mobility literature (Marx, Strumsky & Fleming on non-competes).
→ *Question: Do layer-3 firms cluster in the same labour market as the layer-2 wreckage? If yes, the mechanism is human capital, not physical capacity — and non-compete enforceability becomes a testable moderator.*

**A5. History of technology as a discipline (as opposed to economics of innovation).** Thomas P. Hughes' *Networks of Power* (1983) — the standard scholarly work on electrification, and the source of *technological momentum*, *reverse salient*, and *load factor* — is absent. So is David Hounshell's *From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932* (1984), which is **the** authority on where the assembly line came from and which would settle the operator's example (a) in one afternoon.
→ *Question: What do Hughes and Hounshell actually say about the electricity→shop-floor→assembly-line sequence, and does Hughes' "load factor" problem (Insull's need to fill off-peak capacity) reframe layer 2 as demand-creation rather than overcapacity?*

**A6. Industrial organisation: the shakeout literature.** Steven Klepper and Gort & Klepper built a formal, data-backed model of *entry wave → overcapacity → shakeout → surviving structure* across dozens of industries (autos, tyres, TV, penicillin). This is the closest thing in economics to a *measured base rate* for the operator's layer 2, and it appears nowhere.
→ *Question: Run the 45 cases against Klepper's shakeout model. In how many did a distinct new cohort capture post-shakeout value, versus the shakeout survivors (which is Klepper's finding, and the Capital Cycle's, and the opposite of the operator's claim)?*

**A7. Real options and the economics of capacity.** "Overcapacity is optionality" is asserted throughout and never formalised. Dixit & Pindyck (1994), and Baldwin & Clark's *Design Rules* (modularity as option value), are absent.
→ *Question: Can layer-2 overbuild be priced as a real option, and does that yield an ex-ante test — i.e. is the option value observable before the bust?*

**A8. Development economics: the big push and coordination failure.** Rosenstein-Rodan (1943), Murphy-Shleifer-Vishny (1989), Hirschman (1958, raised only by a verifier). This is the formal model for *why simultaneous over-investment is required at all*, and it predicts overbuild is efficient, not wasteful.
→ *Question: Is the operator's layer 2 a coordination-failure solution (efficient over-investment) rather than a malinvestment? These have opposite policy implications.*

**A9. Ecology / resilience theory.** Holling's *adaptive cycle* and *panarchy* (growth → conservation → **release** → **reorganisation**) is a four-phase model with exactly this structure, complete with the claim that the release phase is where accumulated capital becomes available. Entirely absent.
→ *Question: Does panarchy's "revolt and remember" cross-scale mechanism give the framework the stopping rule it lacks?*

**A10. Military procurement and war economy history.** Vernon Ruttan's *Is War Necessary for Economic Growth?* (2006), Mark Wilson's *Destructive Creation* (2016), Mazzucato's *Entrepreneurial State*. Nobody asked how many of the 45 layer-2 build-outs were **state-financed rather than bubble-financed**.
→ *Question: Classify all 45 cases by who paid for layer 2 — speculative private capital, public procurement, or regulated utility ratebase. If public money dominates the strong cases, the "bubble" framing is wrong and the correct concept is mission-oriented public infrastructure.*

**A11. Sociology of expectations / STS.** Borup, Brown, Konrad & van Lente on hype as a coordinating device; Goldfarb & Kirsch's *Bubbles and Crashes* (2019) was named by one verifier but never searched into.
→ *Question: Is the bubble's function narrative coordination (getting many actors to build compatible things simultaneously) rather than capital deployment?*

**A12. Formal small-N causal method.** Nobody proposed a method. Ragin's fuzzy-set QCA exists precisely for "which combination of conditions is necessary/sufficient across 40 cases".
→ *Question: Run fsQCA on the case library using the seven filters from verifier 3. Which conditions are necessary, which are sufficient in combination, and which are decorative?*

---

## B. ERAS AND GEOGRAPHIES WITH ZERO CASES

**B1. The British Industrial Revolution proper (1760–1830) has no case.** Steam — the canonical GPT — appears only as background to railways. No Newcomen→Watt→cotton mill→factory system chain, no Robert Allen, no "Engels' pause" (the 40-year lag in real wages, which is the *distributional* twin of the productivity lag).
→ *Question: Does the steam/cotton-mill sequence fit the three-layer structure, and is Engels' pause the same lag the operator is describing?*

**B2. The 1920s utility bubble is missing from the operator's own example.** Samuel Insull built the load-factor/holding-company overbuild in electricity, collapsed in 1932, and the wreckage produced PUHCA 1935, TVA, and the REA — which produced universal cheap power and the postwar appliance/suburb economy. This is the actual missing middle of example (a) and no researcher found it.
→ *Question: Reconstruct the Insull chain. Is the real layer 2 of electricity a financial bubble in utility holding companies rather than shop-floor reorganisation?*

**B3. The 1920s radio boom → RCA crash → broadcast networks.** Absent. A clean, dated, well-documented overbuild-bust-harvest inside a 20-year window.

**B4. Post-WWI aircraft and pilot surplus → barnstorming → airmail contracts → commercial aviation.** Absent. Textbook stranded-asset-to-new-industry, with the added feature that the surplus was military.

**B5. No Soviet or planned-economy case — the framework's best control group.** The USSR built vast overcapacity for decades with essentially no third order. If overbuild alone were sufficient, the USSR would be the framework's greatest success.
→ *Question: Why did massive Soviet industrial and scientific overcapacity produce no third-order commercial generation? What does that identify as the missing ingredient — property rights, entry, price signals, or exit?*

**B6. China has one case (solar) and it is the weakest one.** Missing: the Shenzhen shanzhai electronics ecosystem → DJI/Anker/EV supply chain (arguably the strongest non-Western case in existence); high-speed rail overbuild; the 2008 stimulus infrastructure; and Alibaba/Tencent cloud built with **no** preceding telecom bust.
→ *Question: China built hyperscale cloud without a fibre bubble. Does that falsify the necessity claim?*

**B7. Germany: nothing at all.** The 19th-century synthetic dye industry → the industrial research laboratory → pharmaceuticals and Haber-Bosch is a textbook three-layer cascade, and the *industrial research lab itself* is the reorganisation. Also Energiewende overcapacity → negative power prices → ?

**B8. Israel: Unit 8200 → cybersecurity industry.** Absent. A pure skills-residue case with no physical asset at all, which is the cleanest possible test of the human-capital channel.

**B9. Finland: Nokia's collapse (2011–13) → Supercell/Rovio/startup ecosystem.** Absent. Documented, recent, small-n, with government redeployment programmes — the best-instrumented skills-transfer case available.

**B10. India appears once (1991, and that case's mechanism was shown to be invented).** Missing entirely: India Stack (Aadhaar/UPI) → third-order fintech. That is a *public* layer 2 with a live layer 3, and it directly tests the bubble-vs-public-infrastructure alternative. Also missing: M-Pesa (Kenya), Brazil's Pix and ethanol programme, and any Latin American or African case whatsoever.

**B11. Cleantech 1.0 (2008–2013) — the completed modern arc nobody used.** Solyndra, A123, Fisker, Better Place. Capital destroyed, engineers dispersed to Tesla/QuantumScape/Sila, A123 assets bought by Wanxiang. Full cycle, well documented, recent enough to trace people.
→ *Question: Trace where the cleantech-1.0 engineers and assets went. Did the residue enable the 2015-2025 battery/EV generation, or did that come from Asian cell manufacturers who never had a bust?*

**B12. The 1999–2002 merchant power / "dash for gas" bubble.** Enron, Calpine, Mirant, Williams — a multi-hundred-billion-dollar CCGT overbuild followed by mass bankruptcy and stranded turbines. Who harvested it, and is it the closest structural analogue to the current AI datacentre power problem? Absent.

**B13. Iridium/Globalstar/Teledesic (1999–2002).** LEO satellite constellations built, bankrupted, sold for cents (Iridium's $5bn network sold for ~$25m). A near-perfect natural experiment and completely absent.

**B14. The 2000 genomics bubble.** Celera, Incyte, Human Genome Sciences — a bubble that built sequencing capacity and skills, crashed, and was followed a decade later by Illumina/23andMe/CRISPR. Structurally identical to dot-com and absent.

**B15. The ASP wave (1998–2001) — the missing negative-then-positive control.** Application Service Providers were SaaS, five years early, and all died. Same idea, layer 2 failed, layer 3 succeeded.
→ *Question: What changed between ASPs (1999, failed) and SaaS (2006, succeeded)? If the answer is bandwidth price, that is the strongest single piece of support in the whole programme. If it is browser capability or billing models, the fibre story loses its load.*

## C. NAMED CONCEPTS THAT SHOULD OBVIOUSLY BE IN THE LIST AND ARE NOT

**C1. FORDISM.** The operator's example (a) third order has an established name — Fordism — and it is not among the 74 entries. Nor is the entire French Régulation School (Aglietta, Boyer, Lipietz) whose subject *is* the succession of accumulation regimes and their crises, nor Gramsci's "Americanism and Fordism", nor post-Fordism, nor Piore & Sabel's *The Second Industrial Divide* (1984) — a book-length theory of exactly this kind of transition. This is the single most conspicuous naming failure in the programme.

**C2. Generativity (Zittrain, 2008).** The precise established term for verifier 3's filter #1 ("substrate, not product") — why a general-purpose platform yields applications its builders never imagined. Absent.

**C3. Dominant design / era of ferment (Utterback & Abernathy; Tushman & Anderson 1986).** This is the real, established version of what the fabricated "Three Derivatives of Innovation" entry was groping at. Absent.

**C4. Wright's Law / experience curves, and Farmer & Lafond (2016) on their forecastability.** Multiple cases turn on cost-curve threshold crossings, and nobody named the law that governs them — or the empirical result that **technology cost curves are statistically forecastable**, which directly contradicts the "unpredictable" claim and hands the operator his only genuinely prospective instrument.

**C5. Absorptive capacity (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990).** Why some actors can exploit a residue and others cannot. Absent, and it is the missing explanation for the "different people" feature.

**C6. Conservation of attractive profits (Christensen) and "commoditise your complement" (Spolsky).** The two established accounts of *why value migrates to the adjacent layer when one layer is commoditised*. The list contains a misattributed "Value Migration" entry instead.

**C7. Infrastructure as commons (Frischmann, 2012).** Book-length treatment of why infrastructure generates spillovers its owner cannot capture. Absent — and it is the best answer to "why does layer 1/2 fail to capture value".

**C8. Product space / economic complexity (Hausmann & Hidalgo).** A *measurable, published* version of the adjacent possible, with data covering every country since 1962. It converts "layer 3 follows from layer 2 capabilities" from metaphor into a quantity.
→ *Question: Can layer-3 emergence be predicted using product-space proximity from the layer-2 capability set? This is the one operationalisation on offer that could make the framework prospective.*

**C9. The Perez counter-literature.** Not one critic of long waves or of Perez was cited. Rosenberg & Frischtak (1984), *Long Waves: A Critical Appraisal*, is the canonical demolition, and it was written by the same Rosenberg the verifiers say is missing.

**C10. Also absent:** Kindleberger (*Manias, Panics and Crashes*), Garber (*Famous First Bubbles*), Chandler (*The Visible Hand*, *Scale and Scope*), JoAnne Yates (*Control Through Communication*), Vaclav Smil (*Creating the Twentieth Century*), Alfred Marshall, and George Gilder's *Telecosm* (see D6).

## D. LOAD-BEARING CLAIMS NOBODY VERIFIED

**D1. Counterfactual necessity — the whole framework's foundation.** Verifier 3 named it and no one tested it.
→ *Question: For each strong case, find a comparable economy or firm that got layer 3 **without** the layer-2 bubble. Korea/Japan broadband, Chinese cloud, and Nordic mobile are the obvious tests.*

**D2. Nobody ever measured the value distribution across layers — for any case.** "Most of the value accrues at layer 3, to different people" is asserted 45 times and quantified zero times.
→ *Question: For the internet cascade, compute cumulative capital invested and cumulative economic profit by layer (backbone carriers vs CDN/cloud vs application). Is the layer-3 share actually larger?*

**D3. The lag was never operationally defined, let alone measured.** "20–50 years" survived twelve researchers without anyone specifying the two endpoints.
→ *Question: Define lag as (founding date of the largest layer-3 firm) − (peak-capex year of layer 2), compute it for all 45 cases, and publish the distribution. Is the operator's 20–50 even in the interquartile range?*

**D4. The physical survival rate of the fibre — the programme's central empirical datum — is unknown.**
→ *Question: What fraction of the strands laid in the US 1996–2001 had been lit by 2010, by whom, and what share of AWS's, Google's and Netflix's cost base did acquired-versus-newly-built fibre represent?*

**D5. The dot-com "skills residue" claim was never tested and the available evidence points the other way.** US computer science degree production **collapsed** roughly 40–50% between 2000 and 2007. A bubble that destroys the training pipeline is a strange source of skills abundance.
→ *Question: What actually happened to US CS enrolment and software employment 1999–2007, and can a skills-residue claim survive it? Trace, via employment or patent-inventor data, where WorldCom/Global Crossing/Excite@Home engineers actually went.*

**D6. Nobody searched for ex-ante predictions — and the "never predicted" claim is the framework's most damaging concession.** Three verifiers assert no one ever forecast a third order in advance. None of them looked. George Gilder's *Telecosm* (2000) explicitly forecast bandwidth abundance and its consequences; Bezos's documented 2003 reasoning for AWS is on the record; Carver Mead and Metcalfe made similar calls.
→ *Question: Systematically search 1998–2003 publications for forecasts of streaming/cloud/CDN premised on collapsing bandwidth prices. If such forecasts exist and were roughly right, the unfalsifiability charge is substantially weakened; if they exist and were wrong in specifics but right in kind, that calibrates what the framework can and cannot deliver.*

**D7. The demand side was never considered — all 45 cases are supply-side stories.**
→ *Question: For streaming, was the binding constraint backbone bandwidth (bubble residue) or last-mile broadband penetration (DOCSIS/DSL built 2003–2010 with fresh cable-company capital, not bubble residue)? If it was last-mile, the operator's canonical example (b) collapses.*

**D8. No base rate, no denominator, no sampling frame.** Named by verifier 3, unaddressed by anyone.
→ *Question: Construct a pre-registered list of every infrastructure or capacity boom exceeding some threshold (say 1% of GDP, or 3x trend sectoral capex) since 1800, classify outcomes blind to the thesis, and report the hit rate.*

**D9. "Overcapacity" has no operational definition anywhere in the corpus** — despite Federal Reserve G.17 capacity utilisation data existing back to 1948.
→ *Question: Define layer 2 as a measurable state (utilisation below X% for Y years, or capex/revenue above Z sigma) and re-classify the cases mechanically. How many survive?*

**D10. Nobody asked who bore the loss.** If layer 2 is financed by pension funds and retail investors and layer 3 accrues to concentrated founders and VCs, the framework describes a regressive wealth transfer, not value creation.
→ *Question: For railway mania, dot-com and the fibre bust, who held the equity at the top — and is the "third derivative" partly a distributional transfer dressed as a productivity story?*

**D11. No stopping rule and no layer 4.** Verifier 2 proved layers are indexical; nobody asked the obvious follow-up.
→ *Question: What is layer 4 of electricity? If the answer is "anything", the ordinal is empty and the framework should be restated as a set of conditions on a single transition rather than a count.*

## E. WHICH OPERATOR EXAMPLE WAS ACCEPTED UNCRITICALLY

**E1. The tail of example (a) — "cheap mass-produced cars → US built military capacity in WWII in record time" — received zero scrutiny from twelve researchers and three verifiers.** Every critic attacked the electricity→assembly-line link and stopped there. Mark Wilson's *Destructive Creation* (2016) argues most WWII munitions plant was government-built and government-financed (Defense Plant Corporation), and Willow Run is the standard example of mass-production technique **failing** when transplanted to aircraft.
→ *Question: What share of 1941–45 US munitions output came from converted commercial automotive plant versus purpose-built federally financed facilities, and did Ford-style moving-line technique actually transfer, or did it have to be substantially reinvented?*

**E2. The "dot-com bubble" half of example (b) — as distinct from the fibre half — was never examined by anyone.** The operator claims two bubbles built two things: fibre (physical) and skills. All fifteen agents examined the fibre. See D5.

**E3. Nobody pinned the clock start on either example, which makes the lag unfalsifiable.** "Invention of electricity" is not an event; the internet's layer 1 could be TCP/IP (1974), NSFNET (1986), or the Web (1991), and the choice moves the lag by two decades.
→ *Question: Force the operator to name a dated, single event for layer 1 in both examples before any lag claim is published.*

**E4. Nobody checked the ordering at Ford specifically.** Highland Park's moving line ran in 1913; US manufacturing crossed majority unit-drive electrification around 1920. So at the national level layer 3 preceded layer 2 by roughly a decade — unless Ford was an early electrification adopter, in which case Ford is an outlier and not evidence of diffusion at all.
→ *Question: What drive system did Highland Park use in 1913, and was Ford in the first decile of electrified plants? Either answer damages the example; the operator needs to know which one.*

## F. TWO PROCESS GAPS

**F1. No one asked what decision this framework is supposed to support.** Investment allocation, corporate strategy, and public policy require different things from it — and verifier 3's conclusion (that the only defensible product is *ex-ante exclusion*, not selection) is only assessable against a stated use.

**F2. No one attempted the one thing that would settle the falsifiability charge: a pre-registered forward prediction.** The AI datacentre / power / GPU build-out is layer 2 in real time.
→ *Question: Write down now, with dates and named failure conditions, what the framework predicts about which assets from the 2023–2027 AI capex cycle will transfer to whom, at what discount, and enabling which already-demonstrated-but-price-blocked application. Publish it before the outcome. Nothing else in this programme can answer whether the framework is descriptive or predictive.*
